utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Your Honour, may I deal with an administrative matter first of all. I've spoken to my learned friends in relation to timetable. There is no problems in relation to the witnesses this week, as far as we're aware. We're wondering whether it is possible for the Court to indicate that if there is to be a commencement of the Defence case, whether it will be after the break or whether it is the Court's intention prior to the break, which I believe in the second week of August -- second week of July, running through to the first week of August. We have matters that we would wish to put in tow, and clearly the timetable affects us directly. One small example that I can give the Court is that Mr. Smith leaves OTP on the 7th of July. And clearly if I have to get a replacement I'm going to have to make sure that that replacement, once again, is familiar with the case and familiar with the documentation, because it will be required for cross-examination. That is one small example of the problems that we face. But I think on a more general basis the Defence, and they can argue the point themselves, the Defence would wish to know whether in actual fact it is the Court's intention to commence before the recess, if that is appropriate. And any indication by the Court today would be extremely helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, that was one of the matters which we specifically reserved for submissions of the parties at a convenient time when an indication was given a week or so ago. I see there is quite a hush come over the court over this issue. My first question is, are we sure we are going to finish this witness today before we spend time on matters of this nature?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner is dealing with the witness, and we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see from that Brooklyn smile, we are. Yes, okay. So -- well, there's an argument whether it's Boston or Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour may have chosen the wrong B. And regard to Pringle, and Pringle comes back this evening, he had professional obligations, but he has a flight leaving on Friday evening. I have been work out the timetable as directed by the Court. We have one and a half sessions and we will restrict our examination-in-chief to that timetable as indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good. Well that will work, it will be very tight for everybody. Now we go to the question then of the future planning. Does the Prosecution have any submissions as to the time that it needs? I suppose we start with the question, and I don't want to presume to ask too early, whether there are to be 98 bis submissions or not, and is there any known position about that? I don't want to intrude before the close of the Prosecution case if you're not ready. Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone. On behalf of all three Defence teams, I can inform you that the Defence will submit a motion under Rule 98 bis, believing that circumstances justify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That last comment would be taken without need for specific observation, Mr. Vasic. Very well. And, as has been indicated, the Wednesday of next week will be the day upon which they occur. The Chamber is in the Plenary all day on Thursday. The decision on the 98 bis motion can be expected no later than the Friday. That being so then, Mr. Moore, are there any timetable matters that directly impinge upon the Prosecution's progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, there's nothing. The only matter that we have relates to exhibits from the bar. And I cannot think of anything else. The timetable, we are work being towards Wednesday, and that is the -- that's the obligation that we have. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Vasic, you are in the number one seat, so to speak. Are there submissions you would like to place, put forward about the timetable before the vacation and after?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for giving me this opportunity to state our position. As regards the Defence team of Mr. Mrksic, once the Prosecution completes its case, and their case took nine months rather than four, as initially planned by my learned friend. I fully realise that it was objective factors that led to it taking nine months rather than four. Now, given some changes which occurred during the Prosecution case where we were unable to foresee what evidence my learned friend would be relying on, we believe that we will need quite some time to prepare Defence case, and find a moment that would suit the Chamber and that would fall after the 15th of August. You must be aware that in mid-July, and in early August, people in the entire world take their vacations and it is quite difficult to find witnesses willing to come during that period of time. You also must be aware that people tend to plan their vacations quite in advance, and we didn't know when the Prosecution case was going to end, because the time-schedule was changed several times during the Prosecution case. On the other hand, what we heard here, and the selection made by my learned friend in terms of evidence adduced here and not adduced, taking that into account, the Defence must now make some changes in its Defence case. We expected to hear some other witnesses here in the courtroom; witnesses who, in the end, were not called. Thus, Your Honours, in view of all of these factors and in view of the fact that we will be concluding this part of the trial in early July, we believe that the Defence case should begin at a suitable time after the 15th of August. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you in a position to indicate what length of time you would anticipate for your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was expecting this question. I can tell you something that we wish to do and the Chamber wishes to hear, I suppose, namely that we will try to ensure that our case is as efficient as possible. As for the length of the Defence case, we were able to see in this courtroom that it's quite difficult to give firm forecasts in advance. My learned friend knows this all too well, because initially we were told that the Prosecution case would end in February, and as it turns out, it will end in July. However, Your Honours, I can give you some descriptive information as to the length of our case. Right now we plan to call about 20 witnesses, 20 some witnesses. I think that some of them will testify very briefly, not longer than one session for some of them in examination-in-chief. And should our learned friends show understanding, as well as the Trial Chamber, then we are considering resorting to depositions in some cases, with some witnesses, which would again shorten the Defence case. This is not our final position, I need to warn you. We don't have the final picture yet because the Prosecution case is not concluded yet, and we still have the 98 bis submissions, but these are just some indications. We will do our best to take as little time as possible in examination-in-chief, and also to use these other means in order to conclude this as quickly as possible. We hope that circumstances will be more beneficial for us than they were for Mr. Moore when he was giving forecasts on the expected duration of the Prosecution case. We hope that we will be more efficient when it comes to the length of time. When I said 20 some witnesses, this is the approximate figure. We are not quite sure which witnesses exactly we would be calling. My learned friend, Mr. Moore, didn't call some witnesses from his list, so this has some implications for the Defence. We would have to consider the situation carefully. Naturally the number of 20 some witnesses includes experts as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, you've skillfully avoided putting any measure of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted to avoid putting myself in the situation where Mr. Moore was in February of this year. However, if you are going to press me to give you some indication of the length, I would find it very difficult to be specific about it because I don't know how long each witness would take. But given the number of proposed witnesses, I would say that it shouldn't take longer than 40 days, perhaps 30 days. I think that whatever time duration I give you now I'm afraid may be a case of miscalculation on my part. We hope to do it within 30 days, but I can't say that I'm putting that figure to you based on some reliable factors. Naturally, all that I have said so far concerns the Defence team of Mr. Mrksic. I don't know if this was helpful, Your Honours. And I don't know to what extent I was able to be concrete in my answer. It is very difficult for me to give you any firm estimates and I hope that you understand the reasons behind it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, thank you for the moment. We'll return to you in a little while. I think we should first hear other counsel. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. As regards the Defence of Mr. Radic in terms of the number of witnesses, I think we would present the fewest problems and that would be our contribution to the efficiency of this trial. We think that we would be calling less than 10 witnesses to come and testify here, and I think this will give you a pretty good idea of the time that we would take. This is our contribution to facilitating the planning of this trial. The Defence will certainly take much less than the Prosecution did. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can accept without question your last proposition, Mr. Borovic. You certainly will take much shorter time than the Prosecution. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will try to be clear and unspecific, unfortunately unspecific. I fully support what my colleague said. I need to tell you something right at the outset. And the good news for us is that we are the third team to begin our Defence case. However, pursuant to Rule 65(G) we have to submit our brief listing the witnesses. What Mr. Vasic said clearly reflected the problems that we had. The trial did not proceed in the way that we expected it to in view of the changes that the Prosecutor made to the list of witnesses who were called. We learned of this quite late here in The Hague. Another thing is that we heard quite a lot of new facts during the last 15 days alone. Let me remind you of the testimony of witness P-001. I don't need to go into details, but he said something that was quite new to us. First of all we need to do some serious verifications and research in order to supplement our initial brief. We have been discussing this for quite a long time among ourselves. Thus, the dead-line that you would give to us for pre-trial Defence brief in terms of the list of witnesses represents the greatest problem for my team right now. We probably won't have the same problem that Mr. Vasic is facing, namely tracking down witnesses during summer vacation time. Another thing that comes to mind is this: We were considering calling some 15 witnesses to come here to testify. However, I must urge you to take this number with certain reservations. I've been working over the last few days on this number of witnesses, and it could go between 15 to 20 witnesses. As Mr. Vasic said, a number, quite a large number of witnesses spoke about individual incidents and facts, so in that sense I support what Mr. Vasic said when we hold the pre-Defence case conference to resort to depositions. I have some very good experience in the previous trial that I was involved in when it took us less than a week to take depositions from some 30 witnesses. It worked very well at the time. If, however, Defence decides to call some witnesses, especially witnesses that the Prosecution dropped at the last moment, then those witnesses, in our view, are quite important and their direct examination would take quite a long time, in view of the facts that these witnesses would be testifying about. We also have one expert that we plan to call, and then once again another thing that we have to consider is whether our clients would be testifying or not. Usually that takes quite a long time, their testimony. However, I cannot declare our final position until we complete our Defence brief. But all in all, I think that our case would take a month to a month and a half. It could be shorter if we resort to depositions. And if I may add one more matter, I think this comes on behalf of all three teams. These provisional time-frames that we gave you should not be punished should we fail to comply with them. Mr. Moore took longer than he initially proposed, and I hope the same would apply to us, and you will see our list of witnesses once we submit the pre-trial -- or rather the pre-Defence briefs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I have leave to reply on one our two matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I suppose the starting point will be that I will never ever give an estimate as long as I will live, whether personal or professional. This has taken 125 working days. That's six months. Not nine. The Prosecution case in reality has actually taken two months of evidence. The number of witnesses the Defence seek to call is almost similar to the number that we have called. I think we have called 52 witnesses; I'm not quite sure about that. The case has not changed significantly at all. What we have done, indeed I said at the very outset I would try and do it in 50 witnesses if I could, is I have selected certain witnesses and those witness statements have always been available to the Defence. I think we made application, and received leave to call two new witnesses with the exception of -- exception of experts, dealing with matters that we thought would be agreed, but were not. So the case has not fundamentally changed at all. I am entirely sympathetic to my learned friend Mr. Vasic and the difficulties it is to get a case together. But it also must be said that if they were expecting or the Defence were expecting the case to conclude in April, they have had more than enough time to prepare themselves for a case that they thought would commence easily before the break. And therefore, in our submission, if the Court deems it appropriate, we would be in a position to commence before the adjournment. And those would be the only -- the only submissions that we would make on that. And we'll have to wait and see exactly what happens with regard to the witness list, but on my counting, it's approximately 50 witnesses for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Vasic, can we become more specific with respect to the position of your client? Are you yet in a position to know whether he will give evidence or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, right now I am unable to tell you whether my client will testify or not. I can't give you a definitive answer, I need to consult my client immediately after the Prosecution case is completed. But most likely the answer to your question would be no, although this is not the final position as it stands now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, the Chamber, in all of this, as I think all counsel have heard before, is getting increasingly concerned at the total length that this trial is taking. It's not a matter of fault, it's a matter that a trial which ought to have been relatively short and confined is just edging out month by month. And the people most adversely affected by that are the three accused sitting there at the back, and their families. And those other accused that are sitting in the detention unit awaiting trial. The longer we take, the longer it is before their trials commence. From the point of view of the Chamber, we can sit here forever, that's not troubling us personally. But the effect of this trial taking longer is having an effect on these accused and the others that await trial. So we are becoming increasingly concerned to find ways of keeping this trial shorter. And that being the concern, we, in particular, had been looking at the last week of this present term. That is, the last week that is the second week of July, which is the last week before the vacation. And it seemed to us that it could be possible for the Defence case to commence in that week. And then we would be resuming not the week of the 14th of August, but in the week before that, when the normal business resumes. That would be two weeks, at least, of the total timetable. We recognise that that puts all counsel, both Defence and Prosecution, under considerable preparation strain. But we've been giving early warning of that for some time. And we therefore turn directly to you, Mr. Vasic, because you carry the main burden in all of this as to whether it would be feasible for a commencement of your case in that last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really must say this presents an enormous problem to Mr. Mrksic's defence. And unfortunately we do not believe that this is feasible, bearing in mind all the circumstances that we mentioned a while ago when speaking about our reasons, when speaking about the OTP case, how long it took and how exactly it developed. I would find it very difficult to agree with my learned friend Mr. Moore that there were no changes to his case as they went along. We heard a lot of new circumstances from some of the witnesses who came, and yet we did not hear some other witnesses who were originally on the list. All this puts us in a position where we have virtually no more than a week to prepare for the start of our case and to submit all the relevant documents, the ones mentioned by my learned friend, Mr. Lukic. The Defence pre-trial brief and our witness list. The Defence is facing a very peculiar situation also in terms of our witnesses. I think that much is clear. My learned friend called some witnesses from his list and some he chose not to call. I believe the Defence will need to consider this and see for ourselves whether we, in fact, need to call any of these, to our eyes, crucial witnesses. In addition to the problem that I have already mentioned, Your Honours, we do indeed have a problem with witnesses. We could have told them at the time that we would be starting in April or in May, but now that July and August are approaching, these people will be very difficult to track down. It's as simple as that. They're using their only opportunity to take a long leave. At any rate, I think what we said about our estimate in terms of how long our case would take, based on all these rough estimates, I think we can keep our case within the bounds of what can be considered reasonable, and I don't think the Chamber will be facing any difficulty with that, such as may have been the case with my learned friends from the OTP. I think it would be very important for our Defence, after all this time, 125 days and 55 OTP witnesses, to be given fair time, sufficient time to go through this final stage of the preparation of our case and for our case to begin at a time that would be most conducive to the time effectiveness of our own case. And make no mistake about this, Your Honours, the Defence will do our utmost to be as speedy and as effective as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, there is the three weeks of the vacation in which a great deal of work can be done. You don't necessarily have to have the whole of your case finally prepared when you commence. For example, were it to be the decision that your client was to give evidence, his evidence would come first, and that could be expected to occupy the last week before the vacation. So you would not have problems with other witnesses not being available. If he is not to give evidence, you would need only one, perhaps, substantial witness. If those matters are taken into account, do you still see real difficulties?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence has taken into account the duration of the summer break, and we were going to spend the best part of that summer break making our final preparations, in order for it to be as effective as possible. However, I do believe that the Trial Chamber and everybody else in this courtroom are aware of the need to get some rest at least after the first stage of our trial, which has been quite intense, including the preparations before the OTP case. We have been working at full tilt, as it were, and so has the Chamber, of course. As for the dead-line suggested by the Trial Chamber, I believe that if Mr. Mrksic decides to testify himself, he could do this earlier on. I don't think he will be testifying, though. And ultimately it will present insurmountable problem to our Defence team to start our case before the summer break, as I have already indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You also mentioned a date after the 15th of August. That's in the second week of the new term. Do you see it as a real problem, a commencement in the first week?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when I was talking about the second week of August, I was bearing in mind a fact that I think is familiar to all of us here. 90 per cent of working people in the world take their time off, take their holidays the second half of July and the first half of August. And it's a bit difficult to find someone and button-hole them and tell them not to take their holiday, if this is their only chance to get some rest during the year. The 14th of August, I think you said, was the first day of the second week of August, which I believe would be a time when the Defence would no longer be encountering any difficulties in witnesses making themselves available for our purposes. Most people will have returned from their vacation by this time, and this would definitely make it much easier for the Defence to -- to organise travel and everything else in order to have these witnesses brought here in a timely manner, which would help us to avoid any disruptions to the continuity of our witnesses, and I think that is a situation that no one likes to see as a trial develops. It is also a very important time-saving factor. I will try to keep my witnesses coming in a manner of speaking, and I hope not to be encountering the same kind of problem at any stage that my learned friends from the OTP seem to have encountered at this final stage of their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Could we also observe, you mentioned that if your client were to give evidence, it might be that he would come early. Could we indicate that, as a matter of credibility, the view and position normally taken is that your client should be the first witness called so that it can't be suggested that the evidence of your client was shaped, having regard to the evidence given by the witnesses that he called before. So while that is not as it were a binding order of the Trial Chamber, do understand that if you contemplate calling your client the normal expectation is that he would be the first witness called. Is there anything any other counsel wishes to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We will join Mr. Vasic with our submission. Although these would be Mr. Vasic's witnesses, we would find it difficult to start before the summer break. There are some interrelations between some of Mr. Vasic's witnesses and some of our witnesses, and I would like to be given a chance to do some research. There's another thing. Unfortunately we know that Serbia and Montenegro are no longer together. This country no longer exists. The council of ministers has been disbanded. And this leaves the Official Secrets Act situation unclear. There is a vacuum, as it were, in terms of decision making on how this ban is lifted, the ban on military secrets; what the procedure is technically speaking. We have many witnesses coming who will need to go through this procedure, who will need to have the ban lifted for their purposes, for the purposes of their testimony. This might take some time. If that time is not allowed, I'm sure that their testimony will be much the poorer. As for everything else, I think we can be relatively speedy and efficient in conducting our case. If my client decides to testify, that will not change much, because a total of our witnesses will probably not go beyond a number of 10. We are in a hurry; you're quite right when you point that out, Your Honours. That is in the best interests of our client. And I think roughly speaking we should wrap this up as quickly as possible and have a judgement as soon as possible. That is what our team is after. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly I wish to support what my learned friends have said. Throughout the trial we saw the point that the Chamber was making to have a speedy trial, to have the trial over as soon as possible so that they can see their families again and for other trials to begin. My client also has been adamant about this, that we should press ahead with our schedule and not have any deferrals. However, at this point in time I would say what is in the best interests of our clients and their families is for their witnesses to be heard. I do not believe that any of our clients would prefer a speedy trial over a chance to have all their witnesses heard. The Chamber will judge for yourselves, which the important witnesses are and which witnesses need to be taken off the list. But I think we need to be given a fair opportunity to present our evidence, to present evidence that is contrary to evidence presented by the OTP. That is what my code of ethics tells me I should strive to achieve. That is what I believe to be in the best interests of my client and our Defence case. I just wanted to add this as for all the other aspects, I join my colleagues and their submissions. The only problem that we are facing now is the possibility of having to complete our pre-trial brief by a dead-line that is too short to be realistic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will give some thought to this over the next break before coming to a final decision. I think it will be obvious from what has been said that we had hoped to move more quickly than seems to be able to be properly managed by counsel. So we will take their submissions into account and see if we can revise our expectations. I see Mr. Weiner is still there, Mr. Moore. At the end of the last witness there was the prospect of a large number of exhibits that we didn't have time to deal with yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Let me get my notes. Your Honour, we filed a motion to introduce or offer all of the exhibits which are part of -- or all of the references which are part of the expert Reynaud Theunens's report, which is in two sections. The majority of them are military documents, government documents of some kind. Some are books or quotations from books, quotations from documents, quotations from open sources in the press. As the Court knows that this report was disclosed on September 15th in 2005, the Defence on the 30th of September moved to extend its response until 30 days after the report was received in B/C/S. The Chamber granted that request. They received the B/C/S report on the 14th of November, and on the 30th of -- I'm sorry, on the 9th of December they responded. And in their response they listed the three options that they had. And even though they listed the three options, they selected option number 2, which was to cross-examine the witness. They did not object to any part or any document at that time. In fact, over the last seven months they have not objected to any part or any document within the report. It is our view that these objections would be deemed to be waived. However, if the Court is willing to look at the issue, the Prosecution would state that 89(C) places the issue as to weight as opposed to admissibility. A Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it seems to have probative value under Rule 89(C). As stated these documents are largely military documents, government documents, newspaper articles and interviews. All are relevant to the portions that they refer to within the report. And in this Tribunal the practice has been in favour of admissibility as stated weight is the key factor and not admissibility. In the Milosevic case, in the Brdjanin case, various types of documents were admitted similar to these types and we request that they be admitted now. And I would just like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are these the documents set out in Annex A, the second part of that annex?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Of the motion, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Commencing with 65 ter number 5 on page 2 of the annex.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There were three sections within that. One section were the documents that we would be introducing in the court and there would be arguments that would be available in the court. One section were documents that were never on the 65 ter list, and the third section should be all other documents that would not be mentioned in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The first two, I think, are very short, and they're on pages 1 and 2, is that correct, of the annex?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I don't have the annex in front me of me, but I do know the first two are very short sections. One should have four documents which will be the first section; the second should have 10 or 11, I believe 11 documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And then the third section should have a large number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And I would just like to add one more citation, because there was an issue raised in relation to the book, the book of General Kadijevic. And I would like to note that that document -- I'm sorry, the book of General Kadijevic is cited in the decision of Prosecutor versus Dule Tadic, it's cited on two or three occasions. I know in paragraph 116, and I believe paragraph 104, offhand. And with regard to interviews, if the Court would refer to Prosecutor versus Brdjanin, decision on the Prosecution's second request for a subpoena of Jonathan Randall, 30 June, 2003, the Court in paragraph 41 states, "The Appeals Chamber clarified that should the article be admitted into evidence, the author's unavailability for the testimony need not prejudice the accused since the Defence may still question the article's accuracy and the Trial Chamber would have to take this unavailability into consideration into deciding what weight to ascribe to it." So with regard to the newspaper articles, they have been accepted in the Brdjanin case, however it's an issue again as to weight as opposed to admissibility, and with regard to the book by General Kadijevic, it has been an exhibit in the Krajisnik case, as well as the -- I'm sorry, not the Krajisnik, in the Blaskic case as well as the Dule Tadic case, where it was referred to on two or three occasions within the judgement. We ask that all of those documents be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic -- or is it -- I'm sorry, I recall Mr. Lukic indicating that there could be objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have spoken about this, all three of our Defence teams, and I can speak about three specific documents. From this list that bears the ERN number 426 -- [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] "of paramilitary organisation from 19 of October, 1993." [Interpretation] This document was taken off the 65 ter list by the Prosecution in their brief. They informed us that this document was taken off the list, and we never received the document as a result. It may have been forwarded to us as part of an exchange but officially in the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution we were informed that the document was taken off the list that the Prosecution wished to use. The next document, if I understand Mr. Weiner's words, is in reference to 427, which is also on the list. This is the minutes of the 16th session of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which took place on the 12th of May, 1992. This document runs into some 60 pages. I've read the document, and believe me, based on what I could gather, and it is quite an extensive document, has nothing whatsoever to do with our case. I would like to have the OTP state clearly why this document is relevant to our proceedings at all. I believe that it bears no relevance whatsoever. My third objection is to the authenticity of a particular document. This is another document from the 65 ter list; the number is 612. This is a document invoked by Mr. Theunens in his report, and Mr. Bulatovic yesterday cross-examined him on this. This is the interview given by Branislav Vakic. It's from the Telegraf newspaper, and the date is the 28th of September, 1994. I've made copies of this, and I can forward a copy to the Trial Chamber if you'd like that, Your Honours. This is typewritten, this is an English copy, something was crossed out by hand and now it reads "Vakic interview." I don't think newspaper article can be tendered in this form. The OTP should first forward the original to us. I don't even know who the author is of this article, who wrote it. I can let the Chamber have a copy so you can have a look and see for yourselves what it's like. I don't think that a document in this form should be allowed into evidence. This is a transcript of a newspaper article, but in English. I challenge its authenticity. And pursuant to Article 89 (E) the Chamber obviously has the power to impose on the OTP the obligation to prove the authenticity of this newspaper piece. These would be my objections, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. As a matter of principle I object to the admission of newspaper articles into evidence for the reasons that have already been raised. I believe the OTP know about the usual practice concerning this. The author of the piece, or the editor, must confirm the authenticity. We have had, for example, a situation where somebody said they knew who wrote the article, they knew about the signature, they knew about the magazine, and the journalist was indeed working for that particular newspaper at the time. But that was insufficient to have this admitted into evidence. Or in a different situation there was a press conference, the witness said he knew about the substance of a certain piece, he said this substance was not truthful. The article was quoted to him, but this led to nothing. We all know what I'm talking about. I think things being what they are, what has been done so far is simply insufficient for this to be admitted into evidence, and I don't think this piece of evidence can be accepted beyond doubt. I think this procedure, technically speaking, would be contrary to everything that we have been doing so far and to our established practice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. It seems we will conclude in the opposite order from how we started. I have an objection concerning four documents on the list. One is number 485. This is a military expert report of Professor Radovan Radinovic given in the Kunarac trial. I don't think that we can admit into evidence -- the number is 485. We cannot admit into evidence an expert report of a military expert given in another case when the Defence in this trial was not given opportunity to cross-examine. Some brief references from this report were quoted in Mr. Theunens's report; however, this is not sufficient basis for introducing into evidence the entire report of Mr. Radinovic given in a totally different case without giving the Defence opportunity to cross-examine this expert witness. The second document is number 427. These are excerpts from the 16th session of the assembly of Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Banja Luka, the 12th of May, 1992. It seems that Mr. Lukic already put in his objection to this document. I believe that both in temporal and geographic terms this document has nothing to do with our indictment and cannot be helpful to the Trial Chamber when deliberating the evidence. The next document is 468, and my objection is of similar nature. It concerns some kind of an order, number 124 of the Serbian Chetnik movement dated 13th of May, 1993 and published in a paper which is entitled here, "The Serbian Radical Party." I think that an order issued on the 13th of May, 1993 could have no relevance to our case and our indictment. The next objection concerns document 528. This is an information report on paramilitary formations in the territory of Republika Srpska dated July 1992. Once again, both in temporal and geographic terms such a report has nothing to do with the events in Croatia in 1991. These are all the objections I have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Now that we know exactly what the documents are that the Defence is objecting to, I would be happy to respond tomorrow morning, in response to each of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We haven't time tomorrow morning, Mr. Weiner, and I doubt we'll have time between then and Friday evening. I think every moment will be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about after lunch, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That could be more practical. At the end of evidence today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the only other comment I would make is that the Appeals Chamber has allowed in the Brdjanin and Talic case, the introduction of newspapers articles and that's case IT --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the circumstances in which they're used here? Mr. Borovic makes some significant points there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, but in that case it's actually even stronger. The reporter or the author of the article or interview refused to appear. And the Court indicated that even without the appearance of the author of the article the article was still admissable. Which is the same situation as Mr. Theunens, the author of the original article was not here; however, through Mr. Theunens's testimony it is being admitted or requested to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will hear at the end of today, Mr. Weiner, on those matters and then see where the position is. The Chamber has before it now the motion, a joint motion on agreed facts and the addendum which has been filed on the 20th of June, which deals with five of those agreed facts and removes one, and it is the view of the Chamber that both the joint motion and the addendum should now be received as exhibits and the matters agreed to in those will be taken into account in the course of our deliberations. The -- I think that deals with the matters affecting the evidence in this case that are alive at the moment. There is a motion that is aside of Mr. Borovic concerning witness P-024, which will be the subject of decision in the near future. Given the hour, I think the most practical course is to have the 20-minute break now, resuming at 11.00, and we will then sit with the witness through until 12.30. And that will be the programme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the matter of the future timetable, which was considered during the first section this morning, the Chamber has come to be persuaded by the submissions of counsel that its hopes to proceed more speedily are not adequately reflecting the difficulties facing the Defence. For that reason, we would propose that the Defence file its -- their submissions pursuant to Rule 65 ter (G) by Wednesday, the 12th of July. That's the pre-Defence filings. The pre-Defence conference will take place on Thursday, the 10th of August at a time to be determined. And the Defence of Mr. Mrksic will commence with any opening statement on Monday, the 14th of August with evidence to be led immediately following. We would indicate that we hope that the expectations of counsel, that they would be able, by both the use of depositions and other means, to minimise the length of their cases and by considering the lists of the three Defence teams to avoid overlap, that we will able, nevertheless, to proceed with reasonable speed to the completion of the trial, rather than simply lose time by these concessions. And we would hope that, because of the time now given, that we can look forward to a tightly-prepared and presented Defence cases. Thank you very much. We should now have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the motion on agreed facts and the addendum to the motion will be admitted as Exhibit 594.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry that you were kept waiting this morning with other matters that had to be attended to. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you state your name, please?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Ivica Kostovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you are a medical doctor and a professor of medicine?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am a physician and a professor at the school of medicine of the Zagreb University.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you have also served as a visiting professor outside of Croatia including University of Amsterdam and Harvard Medical School; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1976. And then in 1990 I was in Amsterdam, and then in 1976 I was at Harvard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've provided a statement to the OTP as a result of an interview in May 2006?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I gave a statement and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And may the witness please be shown 0600-1985? We have hard copies, Your Honour, too, if the Court would like them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, is that your personal information on the first page, sir? Do you see it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Not yet. Yes. Yes. This is my personal information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, could the witness be shown some of the next several pages, and could you tell us whether or not those your initials on the next few pages?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I initialed all of the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could he see page 10, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is that your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see it yet. Yes. Could you please scroll up? Yes. Yes, this is the page that I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'd like to offer that pursuant to Rule 89(F), Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 595, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd like to move to just a few background questions and then we'll move to the heart of the matter. Sir, you held some positions in the Croatian government in the '90s, 1990s; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't a member of the Croatian government in the 1990s, rather I was a vice dean for science and later a dean of the medical school. I also volunteered in the medical Crisis Staff, and I worked on the basis of an agreement that existed between our medical school and the Ministry of Health. Specifically, I was in charge of a department which was a coordinating body between the medical school of the Zagreb university and the Ministry of Health.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't referring to 1990, sorry; I was referring to the decade. During that decade you were the deputy prime minister for public services and the deputy prime minister for humanitarian matters; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. From 1993, from October of that year, I served as vice prime minister for public services in charge of refugees. And then in 1995 I was vice prime minister for humanitarian matters, and also minister of science.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And finally, you were also an ambassador, if we could say, without portfolio, an honorary ambassador without portfolio for Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for humanitarian affairs. That was appointment I received in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, in paragraph 6 and 7 of your report, you indicated that you were collecting data on wounded or injured persons on behalf of the Ministry of Health. For what purpose was this data, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose of this data and its collection was to see, to establish what needs the hospitals had during this crisis period. Their needs were increased due to the conflict and the attacks on towns. The other purpose was to process any reports coming from the hospital so that there was a pool of central statistical data based on which we could establish the losses among civilians, those who were hospitalised or sent to medical centres. We did that for the Ministry of Health.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the information that you received, was one of the sources or two of the sources the Vukovar Hospital and the Vukovar police or MUP?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Initially we received regular reports from the Vukovar Hospital. Later on, depending on the difficulties they were faced with, the reports would come in less seldom. Due to technical reasons the hospital would then provide information to the Ministry of the Interior, rather to the police station, which had technical capabilities to send on those reports to us via fax so that we received information on people who were admitted into hospital with their diagnosis and so on, but not complete information, due to the difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in paragraphs 19 to 24 you explain how the data was collected after being sent from various locations. Now, the data from Vukovar Hospital and the Vukovar police or also called the MUP, do copies of this information that you received still exist, and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: All fax reports were copied due to the fact that the paper tended to fade. It was affected by heat. And it was then maintained within the medical school archives, together with information from the Ministry of Health. In addition to this, there was a computer in which we stored all the e-mails we received up until the 11th of November, 1991, from Vukovar. Up until that time we would receive them regularly, whenever it was technically possible. There was a man who used to send these e-mails through the postal service and ultimately he was killed, together with his wife and child.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did anyone from the Office of the Prosecutor make copies of some of these documents from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of the faxes in possession of the centre were copied or scanned. In addition, we printed the computer screens or photographed the computer screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. May the witness please be shown 0504-8837. Do you have the picture in front of you, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I just see the statement. I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the document which came from the MUP. It was a fax that was then copied and stored.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you take us to the next document, please, Mr. Registrar? Or the next page. And slowly move through the pages. And then the next page after that, so the doctor can see a few of the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise these documents, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what are they?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: These are the faxes of MUP listing the persons who were injured. There is also the date of injury indicated, as well as the type of injury. I can see it better now because they zoomed in. In addition to that, we can see the affiliation of these persons, namely whether they were civilians or members of MUP or ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know where these documents have been stored, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These documents are currently stored in the basement of the building of sciences. These are the premises that the university made available for this purpose. There are quite a lot of these documents in all fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And are these documents which have been stored part of the archives of the university, or part of the archives of your work, assisting the ministry of health?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to offer 0504-8837.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's been translate add as well, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: They haven't been translated but most of them are names and injuries. Names, injuries, and if -- it will say the civilian or indicate a military officer, if it's a ZNG or some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 596, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is that this is part of documentation of the university and specific schools. These documents were used to analyse the location where the injury was inflicted, the type of injury, and also used to assess the efficiency of the health system in Croatia. A number of scientific papers were published based on this data. Also, this documentation was used by some people to receive the benefits that they were entitled to, such as disability or retirement benefits.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Now, Doctor, were you aware that certain documents were removed from the Vukovar Hospital in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of that. When the doctors from the Vukovar Hospital arrived, those who were not imprisoned, there were 17 doctors and six nurses, among them the chief nurse. Two days after the hospital was occupied we asked them what kind of documents they had. They said that they were unable to take a single piece of paper with them, that they had no documentation on them. And that the Yugoslav army took away eight types of documents with them, including medical histories, copies of the reports that they sent to us, e-mails, then bandaging register, plaster room register, the register of the head nurse. Then a special protocol on osteosynthesis. Why were these documents important for us? They were important because based on them it would have been easier for us to establish the identity of persons. Some of them went missing and our task would have been easier had we have these documents. We had negotiations with the Yugoslav side lasting for about one year. The Yugoslav side signed the memorandum of understanding; however, they failed to turn over any documents to us. Moreover, they claimed that they had no documents at all. We were unable to acquire these documents during the peaceful integration either when this documentation was requested. To this day we received none of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to show you a few documents which were sent to the OTP, the Prosecutor's office, from the government of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness be shown 0344-5949.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this type of document?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have it yet.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This document is a report which the Vukovar Hospital sent to the Croatian Red Cross detailing the situation on the surgical ward. In parallel this information was sent by the Vukovar Hospital to us in Zagreb, to our centre for information. These are the names that were sent to the Red Cross and those same names were sent on that same day to us, or perhaps on the following day. This document was found in the Croatian Red Cross. We don't have this document; however, we have the MUP report containing these names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd like to offer that set of documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 597, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like the witness to please look at a specific document, 0504-8851.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's from the earlier set of documents which you claim are in your archives. It's one page out of it. How is this document related to the one you've just seen? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the document to come up. Could you zoom in, please? A little further up, please. This is a MUP report. On the face of it I can see the same names, Margetic Berislav, Oreskovic Tomislav, as on the previous document, the one that was dispatched to the Red Cross and which was then submitted to this Tribunal by Belgrade. The same names, the same affiliations, the only difference being this document came from the MUP. The Vukovar Hospital forwarded these to the Red Cross and to us as well through the MUP. Obviously, however, the Red Cross documents were never supposed to reach us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, are you familiar with a man by the name of Pero Rabac, Hrabac?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Pero Hrabac. Yes, I am. He is a student in the last year of medical school, and he is helping us with computers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, was he involved in the collection of data in 1991, as part of this Ministry of Health project?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: He was far too young at the time to be involved. There were some teaching assistants involved, such as Novica Radonic from the school of engineering. Pero Hrabac is now helping with the database. He's helping to organise this database and to process data.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the computer which was used in 1991, is that still in existence?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: It is. It had the old system. I don't understand much about these things; however, it still can be used. It can't be used to print documents though, that's one thing, but the computer itself is now 15 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did Mr. Hrabac take some photographs on the screens, of information on the computer?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: That's true. Each of the scans were photographed. The photographs are clear; they can be used. You can see the names, surnames, and personal information contained on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the information, from where does it come, or where did it come?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: The information for this particular computer came from messages that were e-mailed from the Vukovar Hospital. The information in our central database came either from the medical centre, in this case the hospital, or by e-mail. We had a digital radio, ham operator system in Vukovar for other medical centres, but they couldn't set up an aerial because of the continuing attacks on Vukovar and the circumstances prevailing in the town of Vukovar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I'd like you to look at 0600-1955. And just let me know when it comes up on your screen, please.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I have it now. Can we zoom in, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can you look at it --.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could he be shown a few of the pages that follow?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise these?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What are they? Can you tell us what they are?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: These are photographs of the old computer's screen. One can see what basic information was received by e-mail. Name, surname, date of injury, type of injury, and a working diagnosis. Among these names I recognised some whose bodies were later identified at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, these computer screens, or these records from Vukovar Hospital, which are displayed on the computer screens, do these still exist in the hard base or the data drive of that computer?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've brought along some of the originals and printouts for the Chamber's benefit, just in case they should be interested. I have also originals that belong to the medical school. These are photographs, what we're looking at right now on our screens. But I do have the original printouts dating back to 1991 with me which I can show the Chamber, should the Chamber be so inclined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have a view, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I would first like to offer these, and if the Court would like to examine the originals, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You want them tendered as an exhibit or merely inspected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Inspected, copies if the Court would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I asked because I thought the originals would need to remain in the custody of the professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. If we could see them, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Defence may wish to see those.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like to offer the video screens, the 30 pages of video screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 598, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated in your written statement and a bit today how you received data. After you inputted the data did you ever take any action or perform any reviews to ensure accuracy?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, each document that arrived was registered in a special book. It was assigned a number. Secondly, there would always be two persons entering the data and monitoring this process. Any changes that occurred, occurred at a later stage if a person appeared with additional medical documents to complement the data previously received. For example, in October over 100 patients from the Vukovar Hospital were registered and evacuated. They came to Croatia where there were further medical examinations, and then these new documents from all over Croatia would reach this department and we would adjust the diagnosis or do whatever we normally do when we monitor a patient's condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, in your statement in paragraph 35 you discuss what's known as the blue folder. And you indicated that after reviewing that folder you recognised a number of the names. How were you able to -- how were you able to recognise several of the names or a large number of names?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: The main reason that I was able to recognise the best part of these names was that the mothers and parents of these persons had been in touch with me for nearly seven years. They always wanted to know about their children, where they were and whether any mortal remains had been found. That is why I remembered many of these names. I remember the name of Borislav Kostovic, who happens to be a distant relative's son. Doctors told me that he had been wounded. He had been a member of the MUP. Adjustments were made to the description of his injury and his body was later identified at Ovcara. Certain mothers from Vukovar also had their own associations and organisations that were active, and that was another reason I remembered one of these names. I remembered Sinisa Glavasevic because he was a civilian. Virtually all of Croatia knew about him and knew his name. The last time he was seen he was on a bus. It was assumed that he had ended up at Ovcara, so his name remained with me, and I associated his name with Ovcara. Needless to say, when international experts identified the bodies, all of the names were confirmed to be the victims of Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was a letter written by a very well-known politician, if you want to say it, or actually government official, in relation to Mr. Sinisa Glavasevic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the hospital was occupied, and as soon as one realised that Sinisa Glavasevic was not among those who returned, it was the journalists who took initiative and launched a campaign through the world journalists' association. This campaign eventually reached the president of the United States. Questions were asked about this journalist's fate. It was clear that he had been a civilian and also in his capacity as a journalist, there was no reason for him to come to grief. So these were some of the efforts to find out about Glavasevic fate. How would I know this? I wasn't monitoring everything, but I did attend negotiations with General Raseta in Zagreb when I heard about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the information that's contained in this blue folder, where did you receive, or from whom did you receive the information?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: The blue folder contains the same information that we have. Therefore, when I got hold of the blue folder we went back to our own database to do some cross-referencing and find the names. The double-checking consisted in the fact that we had about 100 other persons. We had processed their pre-mortal remains and then these bodies were identified at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The information that you had in relation to the persons that were wounded in -- in Vukovar, did you ever provide that information to anyone? And please tell us when, if you did so, in relation to another doctor.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I understand. Because of the needs of the health system in Slavonia and particularly the Vukovar Hospital, we gave Dr. Bosanac whatever information we had in relation to that area in our own database. In addition to Dr. Bosanac we shared this information with all the other relevant institutions in Croatia. Those who needed to know, in other words, as well as the health ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness be -- may the witness please be shown a document marked for identification, number 345, please. The blue folder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it now. I marked or highlighted the names that I recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is this the type of information that you collected at the Ministry of Health in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We cross-referenced these. On the one hand we were using the book, and on the other hand, we were searching through our database in order to track this information down, and we eventually did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did you determine in cross-referencing the data?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I determined that the highlighted names existed in our computer, in our database. The only names I -- I didn't actually notice were the names of Glavasevic and of Borislav Kostovic. I noticed that these names were missing. Some other names may have been missing too, but those were the two names that I checked in the blue folder.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The names that you recognised, were those people dead or alive?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: They were dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where were their bodies or their remains found?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Their remains were found at Ovcara. I know this because all the bodies have now been identified and we have access to this information too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, finally, this information in this blue folder, is this the type of information that you provided to Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, these were data that we received and we forwarded this data to Dr. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'd now like to offer that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. This document was marked for identification when Dr. Vesna Bosanac appeared for the second time. I ask that the final status of this document not be determined before this witness's cross-examination is completed. We shall try, in our cross-examination, to use information that may affect the final status of this document. I do not wish to go any further into the substance of our cross-examination now, but I would kindly ask that the final decision be deferred until our cross-examination of this witness is complete. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fair, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And one final question. The information in relation to injuries or wounds that you had, could you tell us if that information was ever used to identify the remains at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: That information was used but was not sufficient in itself. A special form was made based on the INTERPOL model, and this form was supplemented by information obtained from families. Families sometimes knew about medical conditions suffered by these persons before their death. In 1994 the Croatian government launched a special initiative in relation to all missing persons regardless of their ethnicity, what fate they suffered or where, whereby the health ministry produced another protocol that was even more elaborate, containing all sorts of personal information, plus the date and type of injury. On the one hand there was Dr. Snow setting the pace using the INTERPOL model and other hand there was a special protocol that the Croatian government drew up in relation to all missing persons and in order to identify mortal remains. It appears that this procedure was successful. Thanks to an amount of antemortal information that we had, the success rate would sometimes as high as 90 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor. I am Vladimir Domazet, one of Defence counsel, and I will be asking you questions on behalf of Mr. Mrksic's Defence team. I will start with the last thing that was discussed. Maybe that needs clarifying, the blue folder or the blue book, as it has been described. What about this blue folder, is this a document that your own department produced or not? I don't think the answer was clear.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: The blue folder is not our document. It does, however, contain information on persons, it contains diagnoses and contains personal information, type of injury, date of injury; the same sort of information as one might encounter in our own database, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, thank you; that was my understanding. You received this blue folder, you used it to cross-reference information in your own database, and then you highlighted the relevant portions. And that's what you submitted to the OTP, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had the same categories as in our own computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the transcript. And then you highlighted the relevant portions in the copy that you submitted to the OTP, the copy that was tendered into evidence, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. First I would cross-reference information to see if the blue folder information was equivalent to the information contained in our own computer, having completed this I would then highlight the relevant portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kostovic, I will now turn to your statement from May of 2006, which was admitted into evidence here. You have it in front of you. It has various sections and paragraphs. Let me ask you first about paragraph 4. You say there, verbatim, "At the beginning of the conflict in Croatia in 1991 a Crisis Staff was established at the Ministry of Health." I'd like to know what marked, in your view, the beginning of the conflict in Croatia, was it a date or an event that you used as a reference?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't I who initiated this; rather, it was the Ministry of Health. There was that notorious crisis situation with the logs involving the helicopters of the Yugoslav People's Army and their intervention forces. Following that there were the events in Pakrac, and that was the first registered conflict involving the MUP forces and the JNA forces. It was obvious that Croatia needed medication. We had no reserve supplies, only the JNA had them. All of the medical supplies were under the control of the Yugoslav army. We realised that civilian population was at risk from various epidemics, shelling, and so on. Later on it turned out that we were quite right. Therefore, we had to have some kind of an institution setting regulations for crisis situations. We had to ensure that we had donations of medical supplies, and that there was a system for coordination within the health system. Naturally it was done at the Ministry of Health. Thus, the Crisis Staff of the Ministry of Health was established comprising doctors, volunteers, including the minister. The remaining members of this Crisis Staff were directors of various medical institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you for this extensive answer. You are obviously referring to events that did take place, but in another part of Croatia. You made no temporal reference, though, and I was interested in that for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. Thus, do you remember what period of time this was?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to point out that these preparations took place in the entire territory of Croatia, starting with clinical hospitals, to medical centres such as the one in Vukovar, or anywhere else in Croatia. This was not specific only for Vukovar. The other thing that I spoke about were potential conflicts and actual conflicts. The conflict in Pakrac took place as early as the spring of 1991. Following that we had Borovo Selo, and other places. Thus, we had sufficient basis in order to undertake measures aimed at protecting the entire civilian population, should there be any kind of risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on your evidence, this staff was busy preparing the health system, as you said yourself, in view of the conflict that was expected, as well as anticipated casualties. Does it mean that you were expecting that there would be a conflict? Was it your expectation, that of the government, or the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: One of the purposes of medical science is prevention. So if we establish that we had no medical supplies, no reserves, no system able to deal with a crisis, then we had to focus on this. We simply had to do this. This was not a military project, no. It was a civilian one, involving universities, civilian hospitals, and so on. We were preparing, or rather the minister was preparing a system that would function as a preventive measure, and it's always a wise thing to do, in medical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. In paragraph 5 of your statement you speak of the structure of this Crisis Staff. You said that it wasn't part of the Ministry of Health or any other government institution, even though you yourself were appointed by that ministry as the chief of this medical staff. You said a bit earlier ago, that it consisted of volunteer physicians. Given the importance that was given to this project by the Ministry of Health, why were these people volunteers? Did they have other jobs and then volunteered within this Crisis Staff, namely they worked pro bono? Is that what you had in mind? Can you explain it briefly?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: The ministry has officials and a minister. It has no operations capabilities. Rather, they did this work via medical centres. In order to strengthen this section for collection of humanitarian aid and its distribution, as well as in order to improve the information system, professor and teaching assistants from the school of medicine got involved in this project. In addition to that, as is typical for other universities, ours also had a centre for human rights. University council established the centre for human rights. This was a partnership where the university helped the ministry. Therefore, there was no professional staff doing this work. Rather, volunteers were involved. There was no order mandating this; rather, these people were given a timetable whereby, if they were not busy in their jobs at their departments, they were supposed to do other assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 8 you said that immediately after this system was established you started creating this network in the field and a central database. Do you remember when this network in the field was established?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: In August. We had a network for gathering information on everything that medical centres needed. We would receive this information from the ground, then the Ministry of Health would assess this information and decide what to do about it. This network was established as early as August. Naturally, depending on the events, we would send more doctors or more surgeons, as needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 12 you said that Novica Radonic gave some suggestions for this system and you said that later on he started entering information into your database. What did you mean when you said later on?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: He wasn't the only one. We had many computer experts from the very heart of our university computer centre. There were even some private businessmen who donated some funds or donated the system that was used. Novica Radonic was a teaching assistant, nothing more than that.
