He entered information into database, gave instructions on how that was to be done, and daily reports were provide for the public. That is to say, that Croatian public and the government could see on a daily basis the number of civilian casualties and how the situation unfolded. The papers would publish daily statistics on civilians who perished in Osijek, in Slavonia and Dalmatia and so on. So this is what I meant when I described this in my statement, that he was a person who supervised the work of other people entering the information into database, so as to ensure that it was checked by two persons. When Novica Radonic was not on duty, then somebody else would take his place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. In paragraph 13 you speak about the draft instruction in a written form on how to report. When was this done?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: It was done already in August. Instructions were given to each medical centre on how to send in their requests for medication or other supplies, and also how to report on the epidemiological status, how to report on their basic -- on their various wards, and how to report on the diagnosis. It's not just a matter of how a person is wounded. What is also relevant is what -- what is the situation in the hospital. Is it overcrowded? Can it admit new patients? Somebody may require a cosmetic surgery, and that person would take up the space at the hospital needed by somebody who had a medical emergency. So we had to prepare hospitals for a possible increase in the number of patients who need to be admitted. This is what we meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. In the following paragraph, paragraph 14, you list what information on injuries, based on these instructions, the hospitals were to provide. This of course includes the Vukovar Hospital. I'm not going to quote all of this. I'm interested in one set of information, which is place where the injury was sustained or location. Why did you, why did the medical establishment need this information on the location where a person was wounded?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: The hospitals received instructions on all the data that we needed for statistical purposes, for processing, and so on. Naturally, not all of the hospitals could comply with this. If, in a civilian sector, during peacetime, there is a traffic accident, the procedure is to indicate the place, the occasion where this took place. It's a matter of regular procedure to indicate where a traffic accident occurred, in which location. This is quite routine. It may be quite an important fact later on for insurance purposes, for any court-related matters, and so on. Therefore, doctors are supposed to enter all the information in medical history. Where the accident took place, whether you had certain childhood diseases, all sorts of information. Naturally, they couldn't say -- send everything to us. They had medical history as their basic documents, and then they sent some information from it to us for statistical purposes. We needed to know whether a certain injury was more frequent in Slavonia than, say, in Osijek or in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but if you are receiving this information from Vukovar, then it's obvious that this has to do with Vukovar. I was just curious as to why you needed this specific identification of the location where an injury was sustained. But I think that you explained this well. When did you start receiving information from Vukovar, based on your documentation?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: We started receiving system information in August. We checked and we saw that we received such information up until the 11th of November, 1991. Obviously we did not receive it on a regular basis due to the well-known circumstances. The last e-mail was received on the 12th of November. I have an example here from the 16th of August, 1991. I can provide it to you, if you want. At that time Vukovar was not still completely encircled, but regardless, we were receiving information even back then. If you wish, I have an original here, and it was still possible for them to send it to us by mail from the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Kostovic, no need to look at that. Based on your answer, we learned when this practice started and, as you say, it lasted until the 12th of November of that year and from that time on you received no information either from the MUP or from the Vukovar Hospital, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to make an observation. We received the last e-mail on the 12th of November. However, Dr. Bosanac was in constant contact with our minister, as well as with our liaison office with the European monitors. She regularly reported on the number of patients at the hospital and their condition. She sent appeals and she also provided information by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, I understand that. But I'm talking about this information that was obtained pursuant to your own instructions and I'm talking about what you received in writing. You said the 11th of November was the last day, right? In your statement you list your sources and in addition to the police and the hospital you mention priests, non-governmental organisations and the Red Cross. Is this in reference to Vukovar? If I look at your statement, it wouldn't appear so. I think in Vukovar the only two sources you had were the police and the hospital, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: That's true. I was listing sources that we considered to be reliable sources, but there were certain places where there were no medical institutions, such as Saborsko, for example, where there was a large number of civilian casualties. It was a priest who called to tell us which persons were killed there, but not in relation to Vukovar. In Vukovar we had reports from Dr. Bosanac; Bosanac through the MUP; we had e-mailed messages; then we had extensive documentation based on reports from doctors and nurses. Don't forget, for example, that there was for example a nurse; 24 hours after she had last seen a patient she arrived in Zagreb. We would take a statement from an independent physician, an entirely neutral statement as to which patients were left behind in the Vukovar Hospital. That was a source, but you're quite right when you suggest that this was not entered into our computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You've been shown this, you identified some of the MUP reports that you received. If we look at the reports we have the names there, the year of birth normally, and a person's affiliation, ZNG or MUP, normally. But there is no other information that you could have used there. It usually says if a person is dead or merely wounded. Not even hospital treatment is indicated or any examinations that a patient was or was not subjected to. You needed more information, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Mind you, neither I nor my associates could change anything about the conditions under which Dr. Bosanac worked. There was a daily average of - I no longer remember - 3.000 shells, perhaps 1.000 shells, raining down on Vukovar. Somebody had to take this information to the MUP and the MUP had to keep the lines clear in order to be able to send this sort of information. There were days when it was simply impossible to forward information, and then there would be concise reports that they forwarded to us that we then used. We had no influence on what went on right there in Vukovar, and there was no way to help information quality, because the conditions they worked under at the time were terrifying. As for those who were evacuated and those who survived, there were usually some medical files which we used to add to such information as we already had. So, for example, if a patient came from one hospital to another hospital, bringing with him his own personal medical file showing any surgery or any injuries sustained, this would then be used. We used medical information only. We used our reliable sources and the MUP was definitely a reliable source, and we always entered information obtained from the MUP into our database.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. In item 22 of your statement you speak about how the list of missing persons was first started, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The time period we're looking at is after the 18th of November. In item 23 you say that because of this situation you decided to make a separate database concerning the Vukovar Hospital to include any data that you already had and in order to update this with new information. My question is, which new information is this based on statements or allegations made by other people that you began these new lists?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: What we demonstrated during our investigation reflects the information in our database. Primarily we are looking at the missing persons here. The missing persons issue. After several days it became clear that between 3.000 and 5.000 persons were missing from Vukovar. It later became clear that about 2.700 persons were brought to different -- were taken to different prisons, Sremska Mitrovica, Stajicevo, Begejci, and so on and so forth. Therefore, we listed all these names of refugees who were in various centres. It was -- it wasn't before the scope of the entire thing became clear that we submitted this information to General Raseta and the International Red Cross, after which we decided to focus on Vukovar Hospital patients. We are the health ministry. We have 400 patients from one of our hospitals, the Vukovar Hospital specifically, missing. We started adding to this information to the extent that we could. However, it -- it wasn't as if we entered something into our database just because a refugee came and said Okay, I saw my neighbour two days ago. The project was about the missing persons. We used universally accepted models to deal with this entire issue, such as the INTERPOL model and other similar ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kostovic, we may be probing further into this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But it is now time for our break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, we have the lunch adjournment now, and we resume at 1.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.29 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kostovic, during your time in The Hague, you talked to my learned friend from the OTP, you gave us some information that had been submitted to us as interview notes. You probably have those, because you have confirmed their accuracy, the 14 items. Some of these issues were raised today by my learned friend. There is one thing that I would like to ask you about, it's about item 12 where you say -- and I assume that this is a book that you wrote; "Mass murder," it's called. In this book, as you suggest, you talked about crimes involving not only Croat victims, but also Serbian victims. As an example you cited the village of -- the town of Gospic. Can you tell us more about this, please?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, this book was written by people working for the information office of the health ministry, and volunteers on the ground who gathered information that went into the writing of this book. It also includes information obtained from other official institutions that are part of either the judiciary system or the health system. Therefore, the information in this book came from health centres and medical workers. Needless to say, when this sort of documentation is compiled one needs to include all sufferings by all the civilians regardless of their affiliation. At this time, back in 1992, because the book to all practical intents was released in January 1992, there was no way to obtain information from medical centres such as the one in Knin, for example, or others. We used Amnesty International information, Helsinki Watch information, and other such independent sources. This was the sort of information that we used for our book. We did not have the same sources, and we would have been wrong not to use these sources. Civilians had suffered in all these other places as well, and we wanted to address that under the heading, "The trials suffered by the Serbian population."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We're talking about Gospic back in 1991, if I'm not mistaken, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember your first statement in 1991, I believe, which was not specifically in relation to Vukovar alone, but in relation to your work in very general terms. You spoke about the fact that between 1991 and 1995 you were the person responsible for coordinating all major exchanges of prisoners of war and detainees. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: That is not quite correct. What is true is that I was a member of the exchange commission, or this commission that was in charge of getting the prisoners freed. For the first three years in my capacity as a physician I attended the talks of the so-called joint commission for tracing missing persons and mortal remains. Therefore, I was a member of the commission for prisoner exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I didn't say that you were necessarily the most responsible person for this, but you were involved. I think you did say that, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And you were in charge of coordinating this. You said you had been involved in liberating over 7.000 persons in this way, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This figure includes also JNA officers who had been detained and subsequently set free. People who had been in detention, be it JNA detention or detention by some of the paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, this figure includes both sides in the conflict, right, and persons exchanged on both sides?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember about the exchange carried out by Croats? Did this include releasing a number of people who been arrested for being involved in the so-called Labrador operation in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: The Labrador group, as it was called at the time, is something that everybody was familiar with. The fact was these people were members of the JNA. This was not part of any humanitarian exchange, to be sure. But the JNA was adamant that those persons should be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, those people were arrested during an operation in Croatia. Instead of standing trial, they were exchanged in one of these exchanges that were organised with the Serbian side, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I repeat, this should never have been an option as far as humanitarian talks were concerned. Nevertheless, the JNA held the most prisoners at the time, and this is what they wanted. They forced our hand, and for us there was no way around this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were you involved in those talks or in that particular exchange? Were you there, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I was there when the 300 people from Manjaca were released and those talks preceded this event. I do not have the relevant minutes or records or anything that I could use to check. I attended talks that preceded the release of the 300 people from Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember a particular exchange during which Vesna Bosanac was able to turn to Croatia, alongside with a group of other doctors? Was this group not, in fact, exchanged for this group that I have just mentioned, the Labrador group?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what other participants in those talks talked about. One thing was the ICRC presence and the humanitarian aspect. A different thing altogether were any deals struck by military bodies. This is not something that I was involved in. When Dr. Bosanac was there, this was only about Dr. Bosanac and Dr. Njavro, that's all I can say. As for any other physicians serving briefly in Vukovar, those were returned as well. And they were among those 17 physicians that I mentioned. But this particular case only involved Njavro and Bosanac. But this was not a text-book exchange, with us there alongside with the ICRC doing things by the book the way they are usually done pursuant to humanitarian agreements or any other agreements signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So what sort of an exchange was it? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: As far as this exchange was concerned, it was a simple as this: Dr. Bosanac was released. It was about her, because it was only her and Njavro that had been held back, in a manner of speaking. Under the Geneva Conventions, there should have been no talks to begin with, those doctors were simply supposed to be released. That would have been a natural course for events to take. For me, that was not open to debate at all. Why were they both eventually held back by the other side? Well, that's a different matter altogether. I don't wish to go into that now, because that is not the subject of my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I agree with you, and I have no further questions in that respect. But were you perhaps there when Dr. Bosanac eventually returned, do you know whether she, Dr. Njavro and the others who joined them on the way back were sent back on a special plane from Belgrade, escorted by General Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: This rings a bell, but I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you very much. Professor, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I have concluded my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kostovic. My name is Mira Tapuskovic, and I will spend some time this afternoon asking you questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I hope Mr. Sljivancanin's Defence can confirm that they allowed me to use some of their time too so that I now have a chance to ask more questions than I originally planned. Can the usher please help me with this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... any more trouble with Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone; the interpreters can't hear her. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostovic, please play no heed to the thickness of these files. One of them happens to be the blue folder which is a document we have already discussed. That's the one right at the bottom of the pile. Top of the pile you can see the orange marks and these are documents tendered by my learned friend from the OTP, documents obtained from Serbia and Montenegro's foreign office. The pile with the orange tabs, if we have any time left, we'll be talking about those too.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last bit of what counsel said.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify something at the outset. On page 31 --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interrupting, Your Honours, because I now see that the interpreters can't hear me.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony in chief, this is page 31 of the transcript, lines 11 and 12, you stated that MUP reports in addition to other things also include diagnoses. If you look at the pile of documents you have in front of you, sir, I'm talking about the orange tabs now, starting with the letter A. Can you please confirm whether any of these reports are marked as dispatches? Are any of these dispatches marked with observations concerning any diagnoses, in Latin or anything at all about anyone's injuries. Types of injuries, starting with the letter A. Can you please look at that. These are dispatches by the home office, and not those forwarded by the hospital to the International Red Cross. Can you please confirm that there is nothing about any diagnoses there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: The orange tabs seem to be about admission to the Vukovar Hospital. They indicate death and injury. There is one death that is mentioned here. This is exitus letalis in Latin, a reliable diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us try both to be brief; I'll try to keep my questions very succinct. We are in a situation where time is a commodity in very short supply. What I want to know about is these documents that you went through with the OTP during these days, documents obtained from Serbia and Montenegro's foreign office. Can you tell us if this is the entire documentation that you received as head of this service throughout the clashes in Vukovar? These documents are now kept at the medical faculty, if I understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Clearly it's impossible to say. The fact is we did not forward these reports to the Red Cross because they weren't sent to us originally and there was no need. The fact is, these names in these surgery reports for the benefit of the Red Cross are also in our own database.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the names now, we'll come to that a little later. What I'm asking now is can you say or can you assert with an absolute certainty that the documents you have in front of you now, which the OTP gave us and which the OTP in turn received from the -- from Serbia and Montenegro's foreign office, is the entire, the complete documentation in relation to the wounded and dead during the clashes in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: This is not complete. In our computer you have an entire database which draws on a variety of different sources and all I can see here is the MUP, the Red Cross --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, fair enough, so you say this is not the entire documentation. Can you tell me this, did the OTP have access to the entire documentation?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. And they photographed the contents of our computer, all the incoming mails from back then, and we saw part of this today.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All we saw were several photographs, a mere handful, but the Defence teams have not had a chance to look at the entire documentation in relation to the admission of patients - those wounded, sick, or dead - to the Vukovar Hospital. When you were going through these documents during your proofing sessions with the OTP, did you double-check the chronology of this information of these dispatches or not? Were you able to ascertain the fact that some dates appear to be there and some dates appear not to be mentioned?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: It's quite right that some dates do appear and some dates don't. There was a two or three-day delay on this information. And at a later stage e-mail messages became irregular. However, we tried to double-check our chronology, even the names, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you warn the Prosecution though that the document, or that the pile of those dispatches that you have, there are at least eight documents without the cover page? For example, documents I'm just going to give you the four last figures, Mr. Kostovic, this is now information for the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution, the numbers begin with 0504.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you don't have to look at that. This is just information for the parties. 8839, 8884, 8850, 8849. Did you draw the attention of the colleagues from the Prosecution that in this group of documents there are dispatches without a cover page or a first page? Did you notice that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: That there is no cover page, probably the documents from the Red Cross, perhaps do not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the MUP documents.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: The MUP documents generally do. And I don't know how much I'm going to make it difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't notice that - is that correct? - and you didn't draw anyone's attention to that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I said the MUP received information from the hospital, and only gave that as an annex to their report. The MUP did not provide us any information that would be sent from the MUP by fax. I know how this could have happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please follow my questions and give me brief answers. So the question is, you did not notice and you did not draw the attention of the Prosecution to the fact that some documents do not have a cover page, and you did not notice that some documents do not have page 2, such as for example documents with numbers of dispatches ending with 8871, 8842, 8838, 8863. Did you notice that some documents are not complete, or that some dispatches are incomplete?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: It's normal because MUP -- actually, the hospital used the MUP fax in order to send the names of those who were received or admitted to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, please, could you stick to my question. No, I did not ask you about the conditions in the hospital or at the MUP. What I asked you was that when you were reviewing the documents which you were probably given to review, when you were preparing for your testimony, did you see that some documents did not have a cover page or a first page and that some of the MUP dispatches did not have page 2? Did you notice that? Your answer can be yes or no. That's it.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I did not pay attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: But what is important is that I said I gave everything that I had, so the question is very clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you gave everything that you had. Did you - you - provide these documents that we're talking about or was it not provided by the ministry of foreign affairs of Serbia and Montenegro, these documents that are labelled with orange tags? This is Exhibit 596.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: All I got was that the surgery documents were for the Red Cross, that this came from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I'm taking you back to what we said were the MUP documents, which, in that pile of documents, begin from the small letter "a." So I provided you with the documents in the order that they were disclosed to us by the Prosecution. The ERN numbers are in -- the numbers in the upper right-hand corner of the documents, and they are consecutive. However, these numbers do not coincide with the dates. The documents that you have are not in chronological order, and they are not sorted properly. So I'm asking you how will the Trial Chamber be able to review the documents and the information in the documents which to them were provided in the B/C/S without a translation? But anyway, you didn't pay attention to that. So you mentioned in the examination-in-chief Exhibit 597. That is the first document that you're holding in your hand.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Page 1, could you please turn back to page 1. Page 1, Mr. Kostovic. Page 1. Page 1, okay. Now, if you turn to the end of that document, could you please tell me how many people are on the list of the Red Cross? How many persons are on that list? 32; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then you told us that the document, the MUP document, 8851 -- Mr. Kostovic, you don't need your papers now, but look at the papers that I gave you, please. Now, could you please find the upper right-hand corner, upper right-hand corner, and that's where you have an eight-digit number. Now, could you please find the document that has the last four numbers 8851. This is something that my learned friend from the Prosecution showed to you on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that that was the same document and that from the MUP list same persons were mentioned on the Red Cross list.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, can you find that page which ends with number 8851 so that we can see whether it is the same number of persons. 8851.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So what is the last person that is on that list?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Stipo Lucic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Lucic, Stipo. The previous document that is from the Red Cross contains the last name of Radacic. Could you please tell me now, on the basis of which documents and which reports, MUP reports or Red Cross reports, did you compile your own database?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I quite clearly said that that document from the Red Cross we do not have because it was not sent. But it is quite clear that the order of the names, and even on that document Sinisa Glavasevic appears, and it wasn't there when I looked at the first page. So it's the problem whether it's the first page or -- but whether we exclusively used at that time the reports from the MUP, we did not have. And I said very clearly, the document of the 4th of November we did not have.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please listen to me now. You now said that you used exclusively the documents?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: For that day. For that day, the 4th of November. Because we don't have the surgery Red Cross document, but we have the MUP document, but you can see that the order of the names is the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there is a difference in the two names?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I must interrupt. The two of you are arguing backwards and forwards over each other the whole time. Each of you, would you please allow the other the courtesy of finishing what they say, and if that is done the people trying to listen to what you say and type a transcript can then hear what you say. Then a reply or the next question. Instead of getting anxious with each other --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is me that owes an apology because it's more my fault than the fault of the witness. So I apologise both to the Trial Chamber and to the witness, because I am putting my questions very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Kostovic, you just said that you never received the papers from the Red Cross. Can you please tell me that the papers that you have in front of you right now, and it's one of the documents introduced by my colleague. Now, for the first time when you came to the Tribunal to prepare for your testimony you are seeing the Red Cross documents for the first time.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: May I now just say that I have seen the document of the Red Cross before. The Prosecution showed it to me, and of course I can refer back to it and say once again that if anything was sent to the Red Cross it was not done at the same time as it was sent to the MUP. Secondly, that is why the list and the number of persons does not have to be the same. And actually, the list never reached the persons or the place where it was supposed to be sent. But these other documents I am seeing for the first time today, these are the documents without the cover page. And they are actually e-mails of what we received. So it is incorrect in my opinion to say that there is no -- that if there is no heading to say that this was sent to the Red Cross. You have now presented evidence, you have actually put the surgery and the Red Cross as a heading, but after that you have pasted e-mails which were actually sent to us. So now I actually know what this is all about; these documents do not have any cover page. All you have is the first page addressed to surgery of the 4th and the 12th of November, and there is no other page behind that, after that. These were e-mails sent to us and now I can show you the original e-mails, find the dates and I can tell you exactly what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostovic, I gave you the documents in the same order that we received them from the Prosecution. I did not do anything in arranging the documents. We presented them to you in the way we received them from the Prosecution. So I have nothing to do with the order of the document, and please believe me that the Defence is doing its best to keep to this original order. But now we're going to go back to something that you said before, and that is that you do not recognise the documents from the Red Cross. Now, the documents that you looked at today from the MUP, the dispatches from MUP, is it true that they were obviously sent to several addresses?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: To at least two addresses.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what these addresses were?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: The information section and probably the MUP. But it's something that I cannot check.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us the abbreviation that appears in the upper right-hand corner next to the MUP dispatch numbers, and you can perhaps look at MUP dispatch number. I will give you the last four digits, 8837 --

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: -- where we also have the abbreviation GSSRH. Am I correct, Mr. Kostovic, when I say that that was the Main Staff of the medical service of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: That is the only thing that this abbreviation could mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you think that then I am not mistaken in this?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, I think that you are right in what you say.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Some dispatches were sent to several addresses. Are you able to tell us whether those dispatches were sent from the Vukovar police administration to those addresses or was it the case that it was sent to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Zagreb from that address after which the dispatch was then sent on to other places? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that going to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction, Mr. Kostovic, you are right. What I meant to say was the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat again that I could not know anything about that other than what is stated in the fax dispatch data. I cannot know anything more.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were told when you were going through this MUP documentation that it was sent to the OTP by the current Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Serbia and Montenegro; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from Belgrade via the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. And you were told that there was a cover letter that came with that documentation stating that it had been found at the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: All I know is that it came from Belgrade and I assume it couldn't have been found anywhere else. Where else could it have been found? It was taken from the Vukovar Hospital. It was literally removed from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostovic, could you now please take this group of documents with the green labels. I know that the interpreters' booth is marked -- the documents are marked with a different colour, but we are now talking about the document marked with the number 1. Could you please turn to the next page and look at what was underlined, what is marked in orange in your copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. I don't have any colour-coded documents here. Could counsel please indicate what she's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Neither does the Chamber, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please -- I failed to warn my learned friend from the Prosecution about the tendering of this document. Actually he was informed in time, 24 hours earlier, but we were actually told that they were going to tender it as well. During the cross-examination. This wasn't done, so now I'm just going to show it to the witness. So I would like to ask the usher to get the copies of the documents, and then the copies that the witness already have now need to be distributed to the parties. For the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution, this is page 2 of document marked with number 1. The page is 0344-5946, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostovic, could I please ask you to read this passage?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: The one that's marked?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: "Please find attached the list of patients found in the register of the Vukovar Hospital in the first half of November, 1991, as well as the list of persons buried in the mass grave near the football ground in Vukovar compiled the funeral home and in the possession of the Ministry of Defence of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the Trial Chamber, that document for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Serbia and Montenegro is translated, the translation is the following page.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostovic, could you please tell us, now that we have already noted that these faxes or dispatches were faxed to some other addresses, can you explain how these dispatches with the reference numbers in the upper right-hand corner were sent to several places again ended up in Vukovar and later came into the possession of the organs of authority of Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer with another question. All I can say is that I don't know how this came about. It would have to be investigated.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kostovic, looking at the MUP documents you saw that some of those dispatches were sent to the police administration in Varazdin and the police administration or police station, and I apologise if I switched either one of those, either the administration or the station. But anyway, my question is if you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Varazdin?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: For your information --

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I did not notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Some of those dispatches were sent to the police administration in Varazdin and the police administration in Karlovac [as interpreted]. Do you know whether at that point in time in Vukovar, among the forces that were fighting there in Vukovar, if there were a lot of member of the police forces from Varazdin and Cakovec?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I know through the humanitarian crisis because a lot of police officers disappeared in Vukovar who hailed from Varazdin and their families formed an association that was intensively searching at least to get the mortal remains of their loved ones. So from the humanitarian aspect, I am aware of what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just an intervention from the transcript, it's page 70, line 15. It should state instead of Karlovac, Cakovec; it's also a town in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to continue. Mr. Kostovic, according to the rules in force at that time, and since you obviously were preparing for the forthcoming armed conflict, what was the relationship of your centre and your ministry in relation to persons that were brought to the hospital regardless of whether this was the Vukovar Hospital or some other hospital, and who were already dead? How did the hospital act and how was such a person registered?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: You mean how was it -- how was the person registered? Well, the procedure was the same as in regular circumstances. It was done according to regular procedure and according to the existing laws and protocols. The only exception was that when the siege was on sometimes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that a person who was killed or who died were brought to the hospital several days after the death in order to establish death?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: People who worked at the hospital also had as part of their duties, that of removing the mortal remains and the bodies. Why? Because several days would pass when it was not possible at all to even go out of the shelter for a minute. So the bodies remained outside. I have the original e-mails - if you like I will show them to you - from Emil Aleksandar who was trying to describe the situation of the bodies of those killed in Vukovar. If you're interested, that's fine; if not, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostovic, I am personally very interested but unfortunately we don't have time, so we will have to skip that. What I would like to do now is to ask you to look at the document in the bunch of documents tagged with orange labels. It's page 1 of document.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For my learned friend from the Prosecution, this is document ERN in B/C/S 0504-8881, 8 -- 8882. This is the last bunch of figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Have you opened that page, Mr. Kostovic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So in the upper right-hand corner, it states 8882. Turn to the next page, please. Can you please read the sentence marked in orange?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: "Today the following persons were brought to the medical centre in Vukovar who were killed on the 1st of October, 1991, in Bogdanovci," and then the names follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't need to mention the names, we are trying to avoid mentioning names here as much as we can. Mr. Kostovic, if you go back to the previous page, this dispatch is dated the 4th of October; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. The 4th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On condition that this is the page that should come right after the previous page, could you please tell me then if it was customary that those killed were brought to the hospital even after -- even four days after the death occurred?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I told you why this was. For four days they were probably up able to and then the service that was entrusted with burial did that with a delay when the physical conditions were favourable to do something like that. So the fact that on the 18th the whole area was strewn with bodies from the Kapetanja onwards makes it possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So could you please tell us then whether this information was then entered into your database?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: If we're talking about something that came through the hospital or exclusively from the hospital, then each person who was established -- whose death was established by the hospital, then the data is correct. If this was done by the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you, in order to clarify this matter, to look in the group of documents with these orange labels, to find the document 632.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For my friends from the Prosecution, this is our 65 ter number 632. And the page that we are going to look at is ERN 0504-8865.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Have you found that, Mr. Kostovic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I do have a 632, and in the upper hand [as interpreted] corner is 8865. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Thank you very much for your help. I would now like to ask you to read what is underlined in orange.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: "During fierce artillery attacks today and infantry attacks in the area of Vukovar and Borovo Naselje, the following persons were killed Nikola Petrovci, Elena Saric, Zeljko Baricevic."

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry to interrupt. Could counsel provide an ERN number. We don't have any document 632 in our system here. I don't know if the Court does.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said that this was a 65 ter document, and its number is 632, I even provided additional information for my learned friend from the Prosecution. For us and for the witness the ERN number suffices. The found the number and the witness read out the portion that I asked him to read.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostovic, I -- I was just told that what I'm saying is not recorded properly in the transcript, and that I'm speaking at a very fast pace. Therefore, I will now read out slowly and carefully the sentence marked in orange in your copy. Or rather would you read it out again?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: "In the course of today's --"

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Unless we can get an ERN number or something we can follow along with the document, it's a waste of time for us. We can't object, we can't respond, we can't redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for your intervention. I can see now that the number is not recorded in the transcript, even though I gave it twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostovic, my apologies?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, once again at your request I will read out 632. "During today fierce artillery attacks as well as infantry attacks in the area of Vukovar and Borovo Naselje, the following persons were killed: Baricevic Zeljko, born in 1965, member of the ZNG, Nasice." That's what you wanted me to read.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For your information this person whose name you just read out is also on the indictment as a missing person. A person who went missing and who was led by force from the Vukovar Hospital. If you take the blue folder, and if you turn to page 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is Exhibit 345, page 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You will see there that the stated person is listed here as a wounded person from the Vukovar Hospital. Have you found that, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us how it came about that a very clear statement in the MUP dispatch claiming that this person was killed led to this situation where this person is listed in Exhibit 345 and then also in the annex to our indictment. Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: There is a very simple explanation. If somebody died and was then taken to Ovcara and then identified, I don't see where the problem lies. Some wounded person and some living persons met their end at Ovcara and it's also possible that somebody who had died previously to that date was also taken there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I need to verify how this was interpreted. For your information, the person whose name you read out is also on the annex to the indictment, and was found and identified. It was buried -- or rather that person was buried at the Novo Groblje in Vukovar whereas in the indictment it was stated that the person was taken out of the Vukovar hospital. Mr. Kostovic, you told us that you and Vesna Bosanac compared the data and this list, Exhibit 345, MFI, and that you compared it to your papers. Did you establish that this person was identified, buried at the Vukovar Novo Groblje, and that MUP had stated that that person was brought dead to the hospital on the said date?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: All persons who were subsequently identified, and this was confirmed by a doctor conducting identification, a forensic expert, that is to say all of such persons were entered into our database. That means that 1.000 persons were identified at Vukovar, or rather 900 at the cemetery called Novo Groblje, then later on all of those identified persons were checked, cross-checked with the database to ensure that there was no overlap. That is to say that the information that Vesna Bosanac received from us, there was no overlapping there. If a person was dead then that that was recorded and following the identification regardless of what else may have taken place. That is to say, if an identification was carried out, even subsequently, then, yes, that was entered into the database.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would it mean anything to you if I were to tell you that this person was exhumed in 1998 in Novo Groblje cemetery in Vukovar and identified in 2001, and that you were unable to compare the data, either you or Vesna Bosanac, to cross-check it to establish at what time and in what condition this person was taken to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: You wish me to comment? I have nothing to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's quite fine.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I can't verify whether what you are saying now is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: For your information, out of a large number of persons listed in the indictment, 14 were found at Novo Groblje, were exhumed and identified. Today we admitted into evidence the statement that you, Mr. Kostovic, gave to the OTP in May of 2006. Together with that statement there came a photocopy from page 11 onwards. Photocopy of lists maintained by your service; correct, Mr. Kostovic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the printouts from the disc. We compared this to the data in our current database.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since this annex to your statement is a rather pale copy, tell me, is it identical to what I'm showing to you now, Mr. Kostovic? This is A-3 format. Is this the printout of your database?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: The printout, what was given to Bosanac from our database, that is to say the same database was provided to Dr. Bosanac and then it was printed from her disc. And then in our database we cross-checked to make sure that the categories and data were identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your database is incomplete. From this document attached to your statement, we can't see page numbers. Therefore, I will tell the Trial Chamber, or rather there are about 3400 entries in your database, correct? Can you please give an audible answer?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But with your statement there were only 10 pages at the most annexed to it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Only 10, because we cross-checked only 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us be specific. I said 10 pages without checking this carefully. But once again, Mr. Kostovic, this is not your complete database.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: What is on the hard disc and what was shown during the investigation is in our possession in its entirety. However, we didn't print all of it. But the entire database is on the disc, the entire one.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now turn to green documents, if I may call them that, Mr. Kostovic. This is document number 2. I am looking for them now. Tell me, please, you have met Dr. Matos, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you had professional contact with him?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I have met him occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Together with Dr. Matos and other individuals you worked on publishing your memoirs concerning the events which took place during the conflict in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't work on having either his memoirs or mine published.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is this a person called Dudas then?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't cooperate with Matos on that issue either. Dudas and I published our system of wireless communication in a scientific journal. No memoirs were ever involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. We don't need to go into further details. Let us now go back, Mr. Kostovic, to your chart. Which is partially included in your statement and admitted into evidence. This chart is entitled, "The wounded chrono," does it mean chronologically?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is computer-speak. It's an abbreviation they use.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So this chart or table encompasses 3.472 [Realtime transcript read in error "3.463] entry, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure you're correct. Is this in relation to Vukovar? I'm afraid I can't be very specific, but that should be the number, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, an intervention for the transcript. Line 23 of page 78, 3.472 entries.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could check the last number and tell you what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I took this from your statement. Believe me, I didn't have the time or the disposition to count them all myself. We have heard Mrs. Bosanac twice. She told us about the situation that prevailed in the Vukovar Hospital. She told us several times, especially on page 594, line 5, on the 25th of October last year, that between 60 and 70 wounded a day were being admitted to the hospital, 60 to 70 per cent of whom were civilians. You regularly, and I think I'm talking about column H, it's a vertical column in your own database. You regularly recorded what is to all practical intents the status of a wounded person, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Adult civilian, infant civilian, ZNG, reserve ZNG, that sort of thing, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did these lists include also persons who were dead at the time they were brought to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: If the MUP said that they faithfully recorded what Bosanac had declared as the exitus, then it must be that way, mustn't it. Whatever the hospital said we took to be reliable information. We used it and recorded it. Because the whole medical system was behind this information. And they had all received instructions to send us reports as accurate as possible. If they said exitus batalis [phoen], then that was what we entered.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So based on just what information did the MUP compile its reports?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac would send a messenger carrying information. Requesting that this be sent to the relevant department. This was when she was in no position to send this information herself because there was just one fax machine. Emil Aleksandar was killed. He was no longer able to send e-mails.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll be showing you some stats now, some statistics. Because you yourself stated that you in a way dealt with the broader problem of protection in these situations that were very difficult from a purely humanitarian aspect, the situations faced by Croatia during the war. If I look at your entries from September, 1991, it starts with the number 465.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Can I have a look too, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: So where would that be?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm just asking you if you know about the condition of your own database.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with its status as it is, what's in it, but that's all we want to know about. We keep this as a database, nothing less and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This list of yours including 3.472 names is something that we studied and the Defence teams have double-checked your entries. Most of this has been admitted into evidence through your testimony to a smaller extent, and it is not very easy to take in at a glance. I'm trying to check this information with you because you are a person appearing here as someone who is supposed to answer questions by the Defence teams in order to furnish information to this Trial Chamber. Can you please remind us that in relation to the month of September there were 716 entries in relation to wounded persons, which averages about 24 persons a day. 357 of them civilians and 359 defenders. Can you confirm that, please?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: If that is part of the documentation, if I signed that document, then it must be accurate. I don't have this at my fingertips, I just said it off the bat in relation to -- specifically. I could go back to the document and see if I can figure it out, but if this is what you got from our own database, then it must be true, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It was taken from your database?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Well then it should be all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Simply because in addition to your list, wounded chrono, we also received a chart showing the figures in relation to the wounded who were received, who were admitted to the hospital at a given time. If you look at this you initialed each of these, about 10 pages. So that should certify the accuracy and authenticity of the information contained therein. We hear that the 4th of October was one of the most difficult days in Vukovar. We have been told many times that on that particular day about 90 persons were admitted to the hospital. Do you know anything about this particular figure, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: All days were difficult, that's what I'd say, depending on the attacks. The number of casualties was usually consistent with that. The 4th of October, yes, the number of those admitted on that day appears to be higher, indeed. Let me find the original fax.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We don't have time for that now, Mr. Kostovic, but, please, can you confirm this: In the month of November - that means by the 20th of November 1991 - the entry in your database is 2400, and it ends with 3130, which means that 730 persons were admitted over that time period, 197 civilians and 533 defenders. I use the term defenders to apply to everyone else. We've heard Mr. Grujic here as well as Mr. Strinovic, and this is the term they used. So we adopted this for -- for our own purposes. If you look at these figures that I've just given you, would you agree with me that in the month of November, by the 20th of November, the ratio between the civilians admitted and the defenders admitted was 21 per cent against 73 per cent in favour of the defenders?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: If your information from the chart is accurate, well, then, it can only be true, can't it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While going through your database there was a particular phenomenon that we noticed. Can you please explain. I'm talking about the following entries, by way of an example: 61 and 62 persons wounded on the same day, the 8th of May, 1991. Can you please tell us how it is possible. These two persons were wounded in the same place in Vukovar, they were brought to the hospital on the same day. The first person is recorded within a matter of days, and the other person is recorded three years later. How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: That's possible. It should be very simple to explain that. People came later bringing their medical histories and files from the hospital asking for their injuries to be recorded. Some never even came there during the siege of Vukovar, some only came later. If they had the proper documents appropriate record was made. If someone was injured, wounded in Vukovar, this person was not treated or registered anywhere, and eventually ended up in a hospital someplace like Osijek, the doctor established the existence of a wound of an amputated limb or something like that, this person later came to our department with the appropriate documents so this would then be recorded. Again, I must say, as long as the files were proper medical files and only then. No exceptions.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell me this: You did not keep any records in your database about persons who were discharged from hospital. I'm talking about the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: A person was discharged. For example, a thousand persons or 2.000 persons, civilians were evacuated during that night. They were bused back to Croatia. They were sent to 33 different towns in Croatia, these people from Vukovar. Their destinies were different. For example, a person reports to a medical centre somewhere and then the people in this centre realise that his wound is related to what happened in Vukovar. This person then gets in touch with our department. However, the crisis only ceased to --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Kostovic, I didn't ask you about the situation after the evacuation of Vukovar Hospital patients. We're talking about this: Throughout the conflict in Vukovar, patients were being brought to the Vukovar Hospital. I'm not talking about the 18th, the 19th, or the 20th of November. I'm asking you a very general question. I don't know about any other hospitals in the Republic of Croatia, I want to know about the Vukovar Hospital. Was a request made to keep discharge records?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as long as a person was in possession of proper medical documents. Any name that was medically treated anywhere in Croatia from the Vukovar Hospital could be added to the database later on. Or information could be modified or adjusted. Your answer is, would such a thing would have been possible, a brief answer, yes, indeed, it would have been possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Based on your indicators were you able to represent the number of cases in which a wounded person received proper medical care and was soon after discharged and sent home to continue treatment, and where?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: It is in bad taste to say the least to speak of medical care in Vukovar over those three months.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I do not believe that the conditions were in place for proper medical care in Vukovar at the time. Everybody did what they could. They just tried to survive and the doctors were trying to keep the losses down to a minimum.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the less serious patients, once treatment had been administered under such conditions as prevailed at the time, were discharged, and is this something that your records reflect? Did they receive outpatient treatment or were they actually hospitalised?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: For as long as our communications system was still operating there is this column in the database, the Chamber has it, this is something provided by Mrs. Bosanac, and we have a copy, and you can see that some of these received outpatient treatment. You can actually see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please go to the document bearing tab OVC 97. For the Chamber and for the OTP this is 97 from Ovcara. That's the number. If you look at the pile of documents in front of you, the ERN number is 0504-8854. For the OTP, 65 ter document 645. Mr. Kostovic, do you have that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I have it 0504-8854.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you. You agree with me that this is a dispatch sent to the Varazdin police administration, right? Can you look at the document, please?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've scan-read it already.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The date is the 1st of October, 1991, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read what appears to be the last paragraph, the underlined portion?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: "We hereby inform the Varazdin police administration that police officers Marjan Jurin [phoen] and Marko Bosak [phoen] sustained slight injuries. They received medical treatment and were subsequently discharged from the medical centre."

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This person whose name you have just read out was later found at Ovcara. We have information indicating that the person named in this document was discharged from the hospital on account of slight injuries. Was this because of the working conditions in the hospital at the time? Was it because the injuries were not serious? But it was the case that they would assess a patient and then following their own assessment, perhaps release, discharge people from the hospital if the injuries were not believed to be serious?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, if you look at the files, it really does follow that this particular patient was discharged. A guiding principle in the field of medicine is that if you have a person who is slightly wounded you send them back to duty, as long as they're a member of one of the units fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostovic, would you take the blue folder now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Trial Chamber, this is Exhibit 345, MFI, and please turn to page 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Have you got page 8?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Line 11 or 12 from the bottom up. In the column on the far left side we can see the name of the person that we just mentioned. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The third vertical column is the date, and it says that he was wounded, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it confirms that the database is accurate. The 1st of October, the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, for the sake of the transcript, you confirmed to me that you found the name that we uttered just a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Bosak Marko.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In this list person is listed as the patient of the hospital. And we have nothing to indicate that he was discharged after receiving medical treatment, and that the police administration in Varazdin, where he was from, was informed?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was from the police administration in Varazdin.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, if you look at the document that I read out to you where it says OVC 97?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Go back and you will see that it says on the 1st of October it was sent to the police administration in Varazdin. Did you try to compare this piece of information with what Dr. Bosanac had in your database?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: If we have in our database that he was wounded and that he was wounded on the 1st of October, we also have his diagnosis and that it wasn't recorded until the 12th of October. Based on that I can't tell you whether Dr. Vesna Bosanac and her team informed us about the further developments. It obviously lasted for 12 days, because it wasn't recorded until the 12th of October. So there was a delay. All I'm trying to say is that we recorded every piece of information we received from the Vukovar Hospital and we did it accurately and instantly, as soon as we received it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. However, at that point you had no mechanism to verify the information provided to you by the Vukovar Hospital, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: The whole system was designed in such a way --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to verify it or not?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: There was no need to do that. The information that we received, what we would verify, is whether we recorded it accurately and to ensure that we didn't duplicate the entries. We had no way of checking how it was done in Vukovar. In principle for us all medical reports are considered authentic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In a situation where a person was wounded for the second time and came to the hospital for the second time, would that be recorded?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Based on our system, it should have been reflected in the records.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm warned that it's time for the break. And if this is a time that suits everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does that mean you have finished or are you still ... You'd better have a word to Mr. Lukic and bear in mind that there is need for re-examination. So you'll have to look at your time. We will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. I am Momcilo Bulatovic, one of the Defence counsel of Mr. Sljivancanin. I was supposed to be putting questions to Mr. Kostovic, and the majority of the questions have already been put by Mr. Domazet. Thus, our Defence team has decided to allow Mrs. Tapuskovic to use our time so that she can continue with the cross-examination of this witness as we will be having no questions for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's very gracious of you, indeed. Ms. Tapuskovic, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Just before the break you wanted to have some indication on time. And my colleagues from the Defence team of Mr. Sljivancanin gave me their time. I think that I shall conclude early enough to allow my learned friend from the Prosecution to have enough time for redirect. That is to say, I plan to finish at 4.15.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostovic, during the break I checked the transcript, and I would like to clarify one thing. I'd like to be more specific. I asked you about outpatient treatment, and you told me that the records on outpatient treatment were kept for only a brief period of time due to the situation; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because later on whoever came to the hospital was recorded in the same way as everybody else. Prior to that there were specific records indicating that whoever had outpatient treatment was discharged as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you confirm for me this: The fact that there were no longer records kept on outpatient treatment does not mean that nobody else following this time received outpatient treatment and was discharged immediately upon receiving this treatment?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: That's your assumption. I have no evidence either to support it or contradict it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just before the break I asked you about a person we referred to as OVC 97 and how this person was discharged from the hospital. That is to say, we will continue with our focus on outpatient treatment and hospitalisation. And also another thing that you said just before the break, namely that as a rule it should have been recorded whether a person was re-admitted to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the instructions that that should be recorded properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now would you please take the blue folder, Exhibit 345, MFI, would you turn to page 39, and look at the first entry, on the 2nd of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, you said page 39?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Which column, first from the top, the first person member from the ZNG was wounded, wounded in Vukovar, and then we have the diagnosis, and then it says, "Wounded again on the 1st of November, 1991." Correct? Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
