utterances.text: I read this out to you because I know that the Trial Chamber has a B/C/S version; therefore, Mr. Kostovic, this type of entry should be a rule, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: It should be recorded in this way as a rule. However, the situation can unfold in different ways. A person can die or, you know, something else can happen to that person, in which case an entry would be different.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't referring to the cases where a patient died. What I'm saying is that we have no records to show that persons who came to the hospital remained there without doubt until the evacuation on the 20th, and that in Exhibit 345, which is to say in the blue folder, because that's the name that you are familiar with, that the only thing recorded there is that the patient was re-admitted, admitted once again. Mr. Kostovic, no need for you to verify this, trust me. It is as I said. The Trial Chamber and the OTP can evaluate whether this is the only entry. 3.472 entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object. We've now gone a full paragraph. There is no question. This is just a speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you see the point?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostovic, can you tell us, do you know whether in the document -- in Exhibit 345, MFI, in addition to this entry there is anything else indicating that this person was re-admitted to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that if I were to believe you, then you are correct. Nothing was re-entered. I can't verify it myself now. In our database I'm sure that this is not a single case of somebody re-admitted. It's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I just asked you about this particular bit, in this Exhibit 345 or, in other words, the blue folder. Now, would you please turn to orange documents. I'm interested in the label, Mr. Kostovic, where it says OVC 45 and 57. Would you please turn to these pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For my learned friend from the OTP, this is page of MUP dispatch 0504-8883.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please read the underlined text, underlined in orange.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I am now reading from the list. "Jambor Tomo, born in 1966 policeman of the police administration of Varazdin; Kapustic Josip, born in 1965, policeman of the police administration in Varazdin." And then it says, the next thing that's underlined reads, "We are reporting the police administration in Varazdin that policeman Jambor Tomo and Kapustic Josip and some others sustained slight bodily injuries. After receiving medical treatment they were discharged from the medical centre in Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kostovic. This means that once again we have another example just as the one we discussed previously, but in this instance we have two persons and in the previous example we had one person. The situation is the same. It is stated in the MUP dispatches that these persons were released or discharged from after receiving their treatment?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were discharged.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please take the blue folder once again. Exhibit 345, MFI. Please turn to page 29. We'll examine that page first. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 29. I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the second name from below. In the horizontal row you see one of the wounded persons listed, Tomo Jambor. It says he was wounded on the 4th of October.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And it is not entered here that he had left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm whether it was recorded that he was wounded again or re-admitted to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you turn to page 33. Same document, Mr. Kostovic.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the only name in the first vertical column, the day of wounding is 4th of October. There is a diagnosis, correct, and then nothing to show that this person was re-admitted to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not here.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostovic, do you have an explanation as to how it is possible that two persons who just happened to have -- happened to be from the police administration were wounded on the same day, received medical treatment on the same day, then they were discharged because they only had slight injuries, and later on they were identified as victims at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: It's very easy to explain. He was wounded on the 4th of October and then he continued fighting or whatever, and then somebody killed him at Ovcara. Or somebody took him to Ovcara, or rather took his body to Ovcara. It's quite simple.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to ask you to turn to the next document with orange labels. Just a minute, I need to check something. This is Ovcara 19. To tell you the truth, I can't orient myself in all of these papers. But this person is not in these documents, this is our 65 ter 729, this is also the person who went missing at Ovcara. Can you explain to me --

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't have this person.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The person is not recorded in these MUP papers. All we know is that this person is listed as missing, he was identified at Ovcara, he is not to be found in document 345, which is the blue folder. We received, however, another document from Vesna Bosanac speaking of how the wounded from the Vukovar Hospital perished. It was admitted into evidence, or rather it was marked for identification - this is Exhibit 346 - and concerning this person it says there that he was treated as an outpatient and discharged. This was stated by Vesna Bosanac. I will give you as an illustration the fact that he was admitted into hospital on the 26th of August, 1991. Would you please look at document 05 -- I have managed to find it. 0504-8896. Have you found that, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we've found that. 504-8896.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is consistent with my notes. Could you just wait a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: It says the Red Cross over here, Red Cross surgery.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Next to that person's name, does it not appear to indicate that this person was an outpatient, that he received outpatient treatment?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it's in the same in relation to all of these, as you can see, the latter half of all these signatures, it says outpatient.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Dr. Bosanac --

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't say the name, did you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The name is of no relevance. The name of this patient is of no consequence to us right now. What matters is how information was recorded. How is this possible? Can you explain why this document should indicate that this person received outpatient treatment? I'm telling you 346 MFI, a document obtained from Dr. Bosanac, that this person was discharged from the hospital. Can you tell me how it was possible ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to this question. 346 has not been shown to this witness. 346 was not discussed in examination-in-chief. It's available for cross-examination, but he should at least have the chance to look at 346, familiarise himself with it. It's not one of his documents. It comes from -- --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Weiner, you've said enough. The witness should have the opportunity to see MFI 346.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. My comment in relation to 346 and the question will be dropped. I will ask the witness this:

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was information verified in relation to this person and was there any coordination of information between you and Vesna Bosanac in order to establish whether this person was a hospital patient on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: All of Vesna Bosanac's information up until that date was entered using our regular methods. There was no further coordination of information in relation to Vesna Bosanac, but at the level of the entire system. It was only once our information was submitted that Vesna Bosanac could probably have reconciled her own information to ours. This appears to have been a case of outpatient treatments. Someone was admitted, discharged and then readmitted without this being recorded but there is no way for me to check this right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Be that as it may, you seem to invoke Vesna Bosanac quite frequently and you seem to invoke the way in which she submitted documents to you. Was Vesna Bosanac sending you her reports from the Vukovar police station?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Not from the Vukovar police station, but rather through the Vukovar police station. This being the only channel of communication open at the time. Under the severe conditions that prevailed, this was the only way she was able to send information. She used the MUP, she used e-mail, she could have used pigeons, for all I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: She used the fax machine at the Vukovar police station. Did she send documents to you using the official Vukovar Hospital stationery?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, yes. I still have those documents. Later on this was no longer possible, and the MUP would just attach her reports to their own reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do we have a single MUP report that clearly indicates this, that Vesna Bosanac approached them with this information?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: That was the agreement we had, and she confirmed the agreement in this way. If you like, I can hand you an earlier report when this was done on proper hospital stationery, so you can see what it looked like when the conditions were still normal. You could have a look if you like.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kostovic. We've seen that, we've seen some of those reports. They were shown to us by Dr. Bosanac in person. These were admitted at the time. There is no need for this right now. But then you need to explain this: Some of the MUP dispatches that we have seen here, some of those that you have in front of you as a matter of fact, were produced based on facts provided by Vesna Bosanac, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. She would send a messenger carrying information to Emil Aleksandar at the post office and to the MUP. This was still functioning at the time, the report was on its way, the postal communication lines broke down, in which case the report would be about two or three days late.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Fair enough. Let's move on to a different subject now and leave the lists alone. Based on your evidence and based on documents which have been disclosed to us which are in relation to you as a witness, I realise that after the exhumation you were willing to allow the post mortems to be performed in Hungary or in Austria, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. We were adamant that everything that was done in Vukovar should be done in the presence of our own experts. We seconded Dr. Kubat and Dr. Strinovic to this operation. Likewise, the EC monitors were willing to second one of their helicopters to us. Later on we struggled to have the identifications done in Croatia. Eventually a team of experts identified the bodies and the same team of experts was used by the Tribunal. We provided sufficient conditions for this to happen in Zagreb with neutral experts present. Of course we never wanted any bodies to be identified outside of Croatia. We have our own experts. This is an entitlement that we enjoy under a number of different international regulations, and this is our own internal matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you please go to document number 6 and go to page 2 of that document. This bears a green label, Mr. Kostovic. Could you look at page 1, please. Can we agree that this is a letter dated the 18th of October, 1993, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is about the visit [as interpreted] of Mr. Vladimir Kotliar, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I need to have a look. Yes, Vladimir Kotliar.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Something for the transcript, line 15, page 98, it was sent to Mr. Vladimir Kotliar, right? Can you please go to page 2, I'll read the sentence out to you. This is highlighted in orange. Five lines down the page. "[In English] Mr. Kostovic has informed Mr. Fenrick today that the Croatian authorities would accept the transportation of the exhumed bodies from Ovcara to Hungary." [Interpretation] I apologise, it's for the transcript, line 21, page 98 -- it's fine now. So there was agreement, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: No, this is about transportation. Transportation to Hungary, well, of course through Hungary. We weren't told that the bodies would be identified there. It wasn't our call, after all. This was a request that we made, but the final decision was down to the UN.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Kostovic, that you addressed the expert commission to point out your concern that, as you said at the time, some digging had been carried out, as you put it, at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we had no access to the area; it was still under occupation at the time. The newspapers and the counter-intelligence services kept pestering the families, the families of victims. It was all over the Belgrade papers, all over our own papers that Ovcara had been dug over. Some high-ranking officials in Belgrade kept saying to the press that all that had been found were animal bones. There was a real concern until the experts arrived and ordered that the site be guarded permanently. The concern, however, was permanent.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The concern still remains, doesn't it. Now there's a permanent guard organised by UNPROFOR with Russian soldiers involved, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: The moment late Dr. Snow, the expert, arrived at the scene the UN soldiers there were asked to guard the site. And then there was the reintegration of the Danube region. So in a way this was under surveillance. We applied on numerous occasions to the UN to confirm that everything was all right. There was one incident described in that book called, "Mass grave." I wasn't there and there's nothing I can say about it. I'm just saying that an incident was described in that book.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. This is probably going to be my last question. Please go to document number 8. Document number 8, this is part of the 65 ter exhibit list and the number is 288. Have you got that, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, number 8, I've seen that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that's the one. I'll read to you what it says. Do you see the title there, 11 mass graves discovered in sector east. Do you agree with me that that appears to be the title of this document?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll read out a sentence to you, I mean the one in passage two. It's the second but last sentence. "English witnesses who had direct experience have said that the dead bodies of detainees had been transferred [sic] From an old brickworks to location Grabovo where some 250 victims had been buried in a common grave." [Interpretation] Mr. Kostovic, did you perhaps have this information? Did you have information to suggest that bodies were later brought to this mass grave, bodies of people who had come to grief in one way or another during the clashes in Vukovar? You were even prepared to go as far as the UN Secretary General in order to launch a protest about this, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I had nothing to indicate that bodies were brought along and buried alongside the earlier victims. We had a list of people who were last seen on those buses. We compiled a list with these names, we had a witness who told us about what had become of those people. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you one thing, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: But we didn't have anything else. We had nothing that was incontrovertible. No incontrovertible evidence. No solid evidence. We only had evidence in relation to the first thing that happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were someone who in 1991, 1992, and 1993 held the post that you held at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Which one do you mean and then I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were at the head of this department that was gathering information?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: It was a section within my ministry. I was there as a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thanks for sharing that with me. But you had no reliable, no verified information, and yet you were prepared to go as far as the UN secretary general with this application, yet you had no grounds for suspecting that indeed there had been a digging over, to use your expression, of the grave at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I will now tell you the truth of this matter. The main suspicion arose because the JNA who had been duty-bound to furnish us information and data who held this information for over a year during negotiations. The word Ovcara was never even uttered. There was a real concern that the perpetrators were trying to cover their tracks, and that was justified as far as I'm concerned. They had been dragging this out for over a year. That was the real problem, not new bodies being brought there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The authorities of Serbia and Montenegro denied you access, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: They did not just deny access to the documents, they denied the existence of the problem.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, please speak one at a time. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Raseta denied on their behalf. They denied this at the meeting in Budapest. They denied this at the meeting in Pec. They said there were no patients from the Vukovar Hospital at Ovcara. They said there was nothing there. They said they had no clue about this. They said "never heard."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostovic, my question was not about the Serbia and Montenegro authorities disclosing documents to you. My question was based on just what do you believe that Ovcara was at one point dug over as you said? Today on page 75, line 15, you stated, "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... and was then taken to Ovcara and then identified. I don't see where the problem lies."

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: That's completely right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kostovic, I have no further questions?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: I want to complete my sentence. Your Honours, may I complete it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think when it comes to this, those who had control over the territory were also able to add bodies to the mass grave. That's what I had in mind, not that somebody did it consequently.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tapuskovic. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You made many references a moment ago. Did you ever request to the JNA about those hundreds of missing persons? When did you make the request, and to whom in 1991, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: The first time that we submitted a request to General Raseta was during negotiations in Zagreb when we handed him a list containing between 3.000 and 5.000 names of persons who went missing in Vukovar. Why between three and 5.000? Because there was some overlap there and that information was not entirely reliability. The doctors compiled a list of patients who were missing, and who had definitely been at the Vukovar Hospital. This was handed over to General Raseta. Later on during the negotiations in Geneva on the 27th of November when the Yugoslav side was represented by minister Gacic and when Vojvodic was a general representing the JNA, I was there as was Mr. Prodan and another official of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. It was on that occasion we signed a memorandum on understanding, we signed a document on the establishment of commission for tracing missing persons, and on that occasion once again we asked that we be informed of the fate of the patients from Vukovar. Following that, every negotiations that we had began and concluded with our questions. We had enormous pressure from the families, from mothers who wanted to know where their children were, whether they were alive, whether they were imprisoned. So we forwarded these questions on every occasion. I received minutes from the International Committee of the Red Cross from the meeting in Budapest where we presented testimonies, both to the ICRC and the Yugoslav side, of two persons who were eye-witnesses at Ovcara and who remembered most of the names of people who were in the hangar at the time. These two persons were saved, somebody released them. They confirmed that this event took place. And we insisted for the Yugoslav side to say what had happened. We wanted them to tell us whether they were dead and whether there were bodies that we could bury; however, we received vague answers that there were many, many events in Vukovar and that it was impossible to maintain control.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Doctor, when was the Budapest meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, in early summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you're familiar with the documents used in hospitals. The 60 or so documents which you were shown which were sent to the Prosecutor's office from the government of Serbia and Montenegro, based on your knowledge of the number of wounded patients, was that the number of documents you would expect to be in a hospital on November 18th and November 20th, 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: No. What the learned counsel directed me to do was to list through these orange-labelled documents. It says here that there were reports sent to the Red Cross and there are also lists of e-mails sent to us, which we have in our computer. All other documents, that is to say case histories protocols of synthesis, register of the head nurse, register of the plaster room. All of these documents are missing, they're gone. And they would have been very helpful in order to identify persons. Now that the identification process is concluded, perhaps they would have been helpful to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were asked about a CD, and you refer in your statement to a CD which you reviewed. And you indicated in your report that you reviewed a sample of some 10 pages. Did you select the number of that sample?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: We established the number of rows in this category, wounded chrono, and then I received the printouts. And we verified in the computer in our database each column individually. We clarified what each column stood for, we clarified if there were any -- if there was any vagueness, and it was only then that I signed the printouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, the question is, did you select the number of pages, how many pages to review?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: No, we did that together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Did you indicate which pages that should be reviewed?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The pages from various periods of time and of various abilities so that we could be sure that it was verified in such a way that it was clear that this was an authentic database, and we did establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you indicated in your report or your statement that the information in your database was identical to that in the CD; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Completely identical. We established that following our verification process.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, counsel indicated that some of the e-mailing, or actually some of the faxes that were sent to you did not have a cover page. Was there any requirement in your records protocol that a cover page must be included with faxes sent to you in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. It wasn't the cover page. It was the first page of the document, which is to say the one with the date. And information as to whom the document was sent. What I asked was intended to show that some documents don't have the first page or we have the first page but nothing else in that document, and we are unable to tell whether the document has one, two, three, or more pages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Analysing what was given to us, I can establish that there is the cover page. It was the MUP who established the technical side of it, what would be there and what wouldn't. It was wartime, after all. And the MUP was part of the armed forces, I guess. So I guess they had some kind of rules as to what may be sent to civilian sector and what may not. What is quite clear, though, is that everything that was sent was sent in the original form as provided by the hospital. And we were able to see that in the Red Cross documents, namely that that document had the same order of data as the MUP document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the fact that a cover page with a date on it or an address on it is not included in your documents, does that have any effect on the statistics or the information that was sent to you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KOSTOVIC
utterances.text: No. It doesn't. Especially since some reports arrived with a several-day delay. What was essential was the medical source and accuracy of the information that was entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Weiner. Professor, I'm pleased to be able to tell you that that concludes the questioning. The Chamber would like to thank you very much for your attendance here in The Hague, and for the assistance you have been able to give us. And we make clear of course that you are now free to return to your home and your work. Mr. Weiner, I did indicate that we would deal with the outstanding issue of submissions, but in view of the time I'm afraid I must ask you to put them in writing. Your face went long. I would hope briefly in writing, but we really have run out of time today and the next two days we anticipate to be entirely taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I indicate to all counsel that I must, I am afraid, because of another commitment, cause some adjustment to tomorrow's timetable. Not to shorten the time available, but to extend both the lunch hour by half an hour and our finishing time by half an hour to 5.00. I simply have a commitment as vice-president that I cannot avoid. It is not a lunch. It is a working commitment. So, for that reason, we will have an hour and three quarters for lunch tomorrow, and finish at 5.00. We will adjourn now until 9.30. And thank you once again for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of June, 2006, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.29 p.m.,
